heading: **ཡང་དག་པའི་བསྔོ་བ་ངོས་བཟུང་བ།**
translation: Thus it is said: From the phrase "if one dedicates in this way" up to the phrase "the Victor has spoken," it is shown that the opposite is the case. In this way, because these phenomena of the object of dedication and the agent of dedication are momentary, they do not abide in the three times, but cease, are exhausted, and are non-existent; the awakening to which one dedicates is also exhausted and ceased; and, in truth, because there is never anything to be dedicated by the virtuous phenomena that are the object of dedication to the phenomena of the agent of dedication, one comes to know fully that there is no dedication. By knowing this thoroughly, one dedicates perfectly without conceptual grasping. Contrary to this, if one makes the object of dedication and the agent of dedication into entities and signs, that is not a true dedication; however, if there is no sign of grasping them as a self, then it is a dedication to awakening. How does one dedicate while accompanied by conceptual grasping? For example, just as eating fine food mixed with poison is delicious at the time of consumption, but causes suffering at the time of digestion or at the time of the result, so too, focusing on white virtues while eating the poisoned food of conceptual grasping is similar; even if it is pleasant at the time of the cause, the Victor has spoken that because it is accompanied by conceptual grasping, it produces the suffering of cyclic existence.

heading: **ཡང་དག་པའི་དོན་ལ་གདམས་པ།**
translation: Thus it is said: From the phrase "therefore in this way" up to the phrase "dedicate in this way," it is shown that one should train in dedicating in that manner. As for the example, it is the mode in which the Victors of the three times understand the nature of the virtue to be dedicated—that is, what its essence is, what its origin is (meaning the causal phenomena), and what its defining characteristics are. Alternatively, one should dedicate in that very way by rejoicing in that which is comprised of the three: essence, nature, and defining characteristics, in that order.

Thus it is said: From the phrase "if one dedicates in this way" up to the phrase "the Victor has spoken," it is shown that the opposite is the case. In this way, because these phenomena of the object of dedication and the agent of dedication are momentary, they do not abide in the three times, but cease, are exhausted, and are non-existent; the awakening to which one dedicates is also exhausted and ceased; and, in truth, because there is never anything to be dedicated by the virtuous phenomena that are the object of dedication to the phenomena of the agent of dedication, one comes to know fully that there is no dedication. By knowing this thoroughly, one dedicates perfectly without conceptual grasping. Contrary to this, if one makes the object of dedication and the agent of dedication into entities and signs, that is not a true dedication; however, if there is no sign of grasping them as a self, then it is a dedication to awakening. How does one dedicate while accompanied by conceptual grasping? For example, just as eating fine food mixed with poison is delicious at the time of consumption, but causes suffering at the time of digestion or at the time of the result, so too, focusing on white virtues while eating the poisoned food of conceptual grasping is similar; even if it is pleasant at the time of the cause, the Victor has spoken that because it is accompanied by conceptual grasping, it produces the suffering of cyclic existence.

heading: **དེའི་ཕན་ཡོན་བསྟན་པ།**
translation: Thus it is said: From the phrase "in this way, merit" up to the phrase "outshines all," it is shown that if one dedicates those merits—in which one has rejoiced in that manner of non-apprehension—to awakening without apprehending them, then, because one is free from the poison of apprehension and practices according to the command, one does not abandon the Buddha, and one also speaks to others just as the Victor has taught. That hero who dedicates in this way outshines all the merit accumulated by any bodhisattvas in the world who engage in conceptual apprehension, through the power of non-apprehension.

heading: **དངོས་པོ་ཡུམ་ཉིད་ཆོས་ཀྱི་མིག་ཡིན་པ།**
translation: From the phrase "lacking a guide" up to the phrase "as if not receiving a reward," it is shown that, like the example of a blind man, if one lacks the wisdom of non-apprehension as the main practice, one lacks the eyes to go to the level of a Buddha. Therefore, because one lacks the wisdom that serves as a guide to lead these five perfections—such as generosity—one is unable to touch the fruit of awakening. When one is fully seized by the perfection of wisdom that is the main practice of non-apprehension, at that time one possesses eyes and also obtains the name of "perfection." The example of how the fruit is not obtained if one lacks the eyes of wisdom, even if other virtues are complete, is like this: even if the work of a painting is fully completed, if it lacks the pupils of the eyes, the artist does not receive a reward until the pupils of the eyes are obtained.

[2-82] translation already produced for this document:
From the phrase "lacking a guide" up to the phrase "as if not receiving a reward," it is shown that, like the example of a blind man, if one lacks the wisdom of non-apprehension as the main practice, one lacks the eyes to go to the level of a Buddha. Therefore, because one lacks the wisdom that serves as a guide to lead these five perfections—such as generosity—one is unable to touch the fruit of awakening. When one is fully seized by the perfection of wisdom that is the main practice of non-apprehension, at that time one possesses eyes and also obtains the name of "perfection." The example of how the fruit is not obtained if one lacks the eyes of wisdom, even if other virtues are complete, is like this: even if the work of a painting is fully completed, if it lacks the pupils of the eyes, the artist does not receive a reward until the pupils of the eyes are obtained.

heading: **སྦྱངས་པའི་དད་པ་ཡིན་པ།**
translation: It is said: From the phrase "bodhisattva" up to the phrase "it is not appropriate," the reason is that when any bodhisattva who has previously practiced the bodhicitta is skilled in practicing the path of the perfections and has no doubts about the realization, then, upon hearing the perfections in this life, they generate the perception that "this bodhicitta is my teacher," and through that result, they will quickly realize the peaceful enlightenment. Contrary to that, when one who has previously practiced the path performs the merit of making offerings to tens of millions of buddhas, yet, because they lack faith in the perfection of wisdom—the essence of the Mother of the Victors—they do not listen to it, then, upon hearing it being taught in this life, that person of small intellect rejects it, saying, "This lack of faith is not the word of the Buddha." Having rejected it, and having become someone for whom there is no opportunity for any other antidote, they will go to the result of the Avīci hell. To summarize the meaning: therefore, if you desire to touch and attain the supreme wisdom of the Buddha, have faith in this Mother of the Victors. If one does not have faith in this, what is it like? It is like a merchant who goes to the Island of Jewels but returns without having found any jewels.

From the phrase "when conditioned" up to the phrase "is not practicing," one might ask: what is the nature of that wisdom? When, by means of the wisdom of the intellect that investigates the ultimate, one thoroughly dismantles and searches through all conditioned phenomena—samsara—and unconditioned phenomena—nirvana—as well as all white, virtuous, and black, non-virtuous phenomena, and finds not even an atom to be apprehended, at that time, because one realizes that nothing at all is established in the ultimate sense, it is counted in the world as the "perfection of wisdom." In this way, the example of the intellect not abiding in any object is somewhat similar to the sky, which does not abide in anything. If it is otherwise, then a bodhisattva who thinks, "I shall practice the perfection of wisdom that the Victors have realized and taught," and who, while liberating countless tens of millions of suffering and devastated sentient beings, perceives the self and sentient beings as distinct and conceptualizes them as truly existent, is a bodhisattva who possesses apprehension; therefore, this is not practicing the supreme perfection of wisdom.

heading: **རྟོགས་བྱ་ཡུམ་གྱི་རང་བཞིན།**
translation:
The essence of the third chapter, the knowledge of bases, is the realization that the phenomena of the aggregates, elements, and sense spheres, which serve as the basis for the path, are non-arising. It is called the "knowledge of bases" because it is the basis for the arising of superimpositions and the basis for cutting off those superimpositions. It is the knowledge of bases because it cuts off the root of the basis by realizing the two types of selflessness as appropriate. Regarding this, there are two: the discordant side, which is the knowledge of bases of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and its antidote, which is the knowledge of bases of the Mahāyāna. By indicating this, it is taught that one should practice by way of cutting off the pitfalls of the Lesser Vehicle. There are nine phenomena that characterize this. That is also stated as:
"Not abiding in existence through wisdom,
And not abiding in peace through compassion,
The discordant side and the antidote,
The application and its equality,
The path of seeing of the śrāvakas and others—
Such is considered the knowledge of all."
Because these are divided by minor sections, they are also incidentally complete; they should be understood in detail elsewhere.

The essence of the third chapter, the knowledge of bases, is the realization that the phenomena of the aggregates, elements, and sense spheres, which serve as the basis for the path, are non-arising. It is called the "knowledge of bases" because it is the basis for the arising of superimpositions and the basis for cutting off those superimpositions. It is the knowledge of bases because it cuts off the root of the basis by realizing the two types of selflessness as appropriate. Regarding this, there are two: the discordant side, which is the knowledge of bases of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and its antidote, which is the knowledge of bases of the Mahāyāna. By indicating this, it is taught that one should practice by way of cutting off the pitfalls of the Lesser Vehicle. There are nine phenomena that characterize this. That is also stated as:
"Not abiding in existence through wisdom,
And not abiding in peace through compassion,
The discordant side and the antidote,
The application and its equality,
The path of seeing of the śrāvakas and others—
Such is considered the knowledge of all."
Because these are divided by minor sections, they are also incidentally complete; they should be understood in detail elsewhere.

heading: **སྲིད་ཞིའི་མཐའ་ལ་མི་གནས་པ།**
translation: From the phrase "the brave one acts" up to the phrase "wanders about," it means: The brave one, the bodhisattva, acts through various skillful means, and by the power of the perfection of wisdom, they have truly passed beyond the two afflictions that are the causes of the three realms, yet they are not liberated in the way of the śrāvakas, who are one-sided in their peace. Even though they have sought out the afflictions of ignorance and views, they do not abandon even the slightest defilement of desire and craving, and they display taking birth through skillful means. Similarly, although they are free from aging, sickness, and death, they display the occurrence of death and transmigration for the sake of the minds of those to be tamed. These beings who lack such wisdom are the aggregates of name and form—the four aggregates of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, along with the aggregate of form—and they are attached to these, which are like a swamp from which it is difficult to emerge. Like the wheel of a water-raising machine moved by the wind, they wander again and again in the three realms and the six classes of beings, which is the meaning of the wheel of cyclic existence. Those beings who are confused about the path are like animals caught in a net who cannot escape; knowing that they are caught in the net of the four rivers and cannot escape from cyclic existence, one who possesses the wisdom that understands non-arising wanders about without attachment or reliance on anything, just as a bird flies through the sky.

heading: **གནས་པའི་མཐའ་འགག་པ།**
translation: It is said: from the phrase "perfectly pure conduct" up to the phrase "moves without attachment," any bodhisattva whose conduct is perfectly pure does not practice by clinging to the object of form, and likewise does not practice by way of clinging to consciousness, perception, feeling, or mental volition. If one practices in that way without clinging, one completely abandons all attachment and aversion, and that state where the mind moves away from clinging and attachment is what the Sugatas call "practicing the perfection of wisdom." Thus, a bodhisattva who practices by not clinging to the five aggregates as being truly existent is wise because they possess the continuity of their training. Being clear through having realized the meaning, they cut through attachment and clinging by their own continuum, and move toward the stage of a Buddha without any attachment or clinging to the three realms of existence.

heading: **ཇི་ལྟར་རྟོགས་པའི་རྣམ་པ།**
translation: It is said: from the phrase "like the sun freed from the eclipse of Rāhu" up to the phrase "practicing the supreme perfection," the analogy for dispelling the darkness of ignorance and burning up the grasping at things is as follows: Just as the sun, when freed from the eclipse of Rāhu, shines brilliantly after having looked past the darkness, and just as fire, when ignited, burns up the objects to be burned such as grass, wood, and forests, so too, although all the phenomena of the defilements and their antidotes, the factors of purification, are by nature pure, the bodhisattva, through the perfection of wisdom that knows the path as non-apprehensible, views them as being perfectly pure by way of the mind. By looking in this way, the agent—the bodhisattva—is not apprehended, and the phenomena that are the objects of observation and the modes of observation are also not apprehended. Thus, knowing the three spheres to be non-apprehensible is what is meant by practicing the supreme perfection of wisdom. With this, the three knowledges, which are the meaning of the view, have been explained in their intermediate form.

It is said: from the phrase "perfectly pure conduct" up to the phrase "moves without attachment," any bodhisattva whose conduct is perfectly pure does not practice by clinging to the object of form, and likewise does not practice by way of clinging to consciousness, perception, feeling, or mental volition. If one practices in that way without clinging, one completely abandons all attachment and aversion, and that state where the mind moves away from clinging and attachment is what the Sugatas call "practicing the perfection of wisdom." Thus, a bodhisattva who practices by not clinging to the five aggregates as being truly existent is wise because they possess the continuity of their training. Being clear through having realized the meaning, they cut through attachment and clinging by their own continuum, and move toward the stage of a Buddha without any attachment or clinging to the three realms of existence.

It is said: from the phrase "like the sun freed from the eclipse of Rāhu" up to the phrase "practicing the supreme perfection," the analogy for dispelling the darkness of ignorance and burning up the grasping at things is as follows: Just as the sun, when freed from the eclipse of Rāhu, shines brilliantly after having looked past the darkness, and just as fire, when ignited, burns up the objects to be burned such as grass, wood, and forests, so too, although all the phenomena of the defilements and their antidotes, the factors of purification, are by nature pure, the bodhisattva, through the perfection of wisdom that knows the path as non-apprehensible, views them as being perfectly pure by way of the mind. By looking in this way, the agent—the bodhisattva—is not apprehended, and the phenomena that are the objects of observation and the modes of observation are also not apprehended. Thus, knowing the three spheres to be non-apprehensible is what is meant by practicing the supreme perfection of wisdom. With this, the three knowledges, which are the meaning of the view, have been explained in their intermediate form.

heading: **དྲི་བ་སྔོན་དུ་འགྲོ་བས་ཤེས་རབ་ལ་སྦྱོར་བ།**
translation:
Applying to the perfection of wisdom preceded by questions is, among the two [types of] peak of all aspects that primarily teach the meaning of meditative equipoise for the purpose of cultivating the method of experiencing the meaning of the three knowledges, the essence of the application of the complete realization of all aspects of the fourth chapter, which is the realization of the three knowledges brought about by the power of effort through meditating by condensing the four causes of the Truth Body and the three types of paths into objects of focus. Since the four applications are taught by way of their own essence, there is no need to teach them by way of illustration. This is taught through eleven divisions, and furthermore, it is also taught by these minor chapters:
"Aspects, together with applications,
Qualities, faults, and characteristics,
Liberation and the counterparts of definite discrimination,
The community of irreversible learners,
The equality of cyclic existence and peace,
The supreme purification of the field,
And the realization of the complete realization of all aspects,
These are included together with skillful means."
Although there is no explicit demarcation by these lines, they are implicitly complete.

heading: **དྲི་བ་སྔོན་དུ་འགྲོ་བས་ཤེས་རབ་ལ་སྦྱོར་བ།**
translation: It is said: from the passage "regarding the Victorious One" up to "the bodhisattva strives," the Lord of Gods, Śakra, asked the Victorious One, Śākyamuni: "Bhagavan, how should a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to practice the perfection of wisdom strive? How should they train in the basis of application that is non-application?" In response to this request, it is said that they do not strive even to the slightest degree regarding any phenomenon, such as the aggregates, elements, or sense fields, and that not striving regarding the aggregates and so forth is the striving of a bodhisattva.

Applying to the perfection of wisdom preceded by questions is, among the two [types of] peak of all aspects that primarily teach the meaning of meditative equipoise for the purpose of cultivating the method of experiencing the meaning of the three knowledges, the essence of the application of the complete realization of all aspects of the fourth chapter, which is the realization of the three knowledges brought about by the power of effort through meditating by condensing the four causes of the Truth Body and the three types of paths into objects of focus. Since the four applications are taught by way of their own essence, there is no need to teach them by way of illustration. This is taught through eleven divisions, and furthermore, it is also taught by these minor chapters:
"Aspects, together with applications,
Qualities, faults, and characteristics,
Liberation and the counterparts of definite discrimination,
The community of irreversible learners,
The equality of cyclic existence and peace,
The supreme purification of the field,
And the realization of the complete realization of all aspects,
These are included together with skillful means."
Although there is no explicit demarcation by these lines, they are implicitly complete.

heading: **སྦྱོར་བ་དེའི་སྔོན་དུ་འགྲོ་བའི་རྒྱུ་ཡོན་ཏན།**
translation: From the passage "regarding this teaching" up to "the remainder," it should be understood that any person who knows that all these phenomena—the phenomena of the afflicted saṃsāra and the phenomena of the purified nirvāṇa—appear like emanations and illusions, yet are devoid of truth; who is free from doubt, thinking that it is not otherwise and that there is no need to train; and who repeatedly applies themselves to training in that way, is a sentient being who has already entered this path of the Great Vehicle long ago in the distant past, and who has previously performed superior service to many tens of millions of perfectly complete Buddhas.

heading: **རྣམ་པར་མི་རྟོག་པ་བསྟན་པ།**
translation: It is said: From the passage "whoever practices this" up to "practices the supreme perfection," it should be understood that a bodhisattva who practices this Mother does not conceptualize the Buddha-qualities as things to be grasped. What are these phenomena? They do not conceptualize the ten powers, the four bases of miraculous power, or the resultant peaceful enlightenment as the dharmakāya. They do not conceptualize them as having an intrinsic nature, but rather practice through the blessing of the Buddha in a state of non-conceptualization, free from specific mental constructions. This is what it means to practice the supreme Mother, the perfection of wisdom.

heading: **དོན་དགོད་པ།**
translation: From "If a mother falls ill" up to "they take care of her," the justification for protection is illustrated by an analogy: For example, when a mother falls ill, though she has many children, all those children, thinking, "Our mother is very kind," become distressed and, in order to ensure that no harm comes to her, attend to her. Likewise, the Buddhas of the world spheres in the ten directions also take care of this sacred perfection of wisdom, which has become their own mother, and thus they protect and guard those who practice it.

heading: **དེའི་མཚན་འདོགས་པ།**
translation: It is said: From "The wise one in the world" up to "is given the name," furthermore, whether the wise Buddhas reside in the world or have passed into parinirvāṇa, this emptiness—the nature of phenomena, which is the faultless dharmatā—has existed from the very beginning. This is because it is said in the Great Sūtra: "Whether Buddhas appear in the world or do not appear, the defining characteristic of phenomena remains just so." Because a Bodhisattva, by relying on the perfection of wisdom, realizes this suchness in accordance with that abiding nature, for that reason, this synonym for the name of a Buddha, "Tathāgata," is also bestowed upon the one who realizes it.

heading: **རྒྱས་པར་བཤད་པ།**
translation: It is said: From "sentient beings suffering" up to "also teaches the Dharma," in general, conventionally, they liberate sentient beings from suffering and, specifically, they completely deliver them from the three lower realms; yet, in ultimate reality, the guide never possesses the notion that "I have performed a service for such-and-such a number of sentient beings." As an analogy for subduing wrong views, like a "lion among men," the Buddha, who is a lion among men, also relies upon the perfection of wisdom, which is like a mountain ravine, to terrify many non-Buddhists who hold to wrong paths, and he also proclaims the sound of the emptiness of the world. As an analogy for following and supporting those who have not realized, like the sun, the King of Dharma also relies upon this perfection of wisdom, which is like the sky, to dry up the water and wind of the body and enjoyments that propagate the seeds of existence, and he also teaches the Dharma of the path to liberation.

heading: **རྒྱས་པར་བཤད་པ།**
translation: It is said: From "seeing the sky" up to "seeing all phenomena," if one asks how they are seen, the meaning of those words that some sentient beings express—saying "I see the sky"—is this: examine the meaning of how the sky is seen. When one looks in that way, there is no seeing anywhere; in that same way, the Tathāgata has taught that seeing the reality of phenomena is like the sky. The analogy of the sky for seeing reality can also be explained and taught by other means. Any bodhisattva who sees in that way—the manner of not seeing the sky—also sees all phenomena.

[2-128] translation already produced for this document:
From "not seeing forms" up to "the Tathāgata has taught," when one searches with the intellect that engages in analysis, one does not see forms even as mere appearances, nor does one see sensations; likewise, there is no seeing of perceptions, nor does one see intentions. Regarding the essence of the matter, from the point of what is accumulated, consciousness and intentions serve as the basis for knowing the mind; because there is no seeing of these, there is also no seeing of the unconditioned, which is the reverse of these. This is what the Tathāgata taught as "seeing the reality of phenomena," and the Sūtra of the Correct Gathering of Phenomena also teaches that "not seeing anything at all is seeing the suchness."

heading: **རྒྱལ་པོའི་དཔེས་བྱ་བ་རྨད་དུ་བྱུང་བ་དང་ལྡན་པ།**
translation: It is said: From "the king in the town" up to "gathered all," just as a great king, even when affairs are being settled, does not go to the towns or the countryside, but remains in his own domain while his ministers gather all the assemblies and so forth, so too, when a bodhisattva is in meditative equipoise, he does not go anywhere in terms of reality, and when in the subsequent attainment, he gathers all that there is, such as the qualities of the Buddha-grounds, the powers, and the fearlessnesses.

heading: **རྒྱ་མཚོའི་གྲུ་ཞིག་པ་འཛིན་པ་དང་མི་འཛིན་པའི་དཔེ།**
translation: It is said: From "entering the ocean" up to "quickly touch," regarding the analogy of grasping and not grasping attachment, any bodhisattva who possesses faith in the causes and has attained faith in the results will not attain enlightenment if they do not follow the Mother, the perfection of wisdom, which is accompanied by method. However, if those who possess such faith are completely seized by wisdom—that is, they possess the qualities of method that desire the benefit of sentient beings—they will quickly touch the enlightenment of the Sugata, which is endowed with supreme and marvelous qualities.

translation: Thus it is said. From "for some" up to "attain the supreme," just as in the analogy of the fired and unfired clay pot, even if a bodhisattva possesses much faith, such as trust in cause and effect, if they lack the wisdom that knows non-apprehension, they will fall into cyclic existence and fail to quickly progress on the path of liberation. However, if those who possess such faith are completely seized by wisdom—that is, they possess the qualities of method that desire the benefit of sentient beings—they will quickly touch the enlightenment of the Sugata, which is endowed with supreme and marvelous qualities.

heading: **ཆུ་རྒལ་བའི་གྲུ་མ་བཅོས་པ་དང་བཅོས་པའི་དཔེ།**
translation: Thus it is said. From "well-crafted" up to "will touch," regarding the analogy of a boat entering the ocean that is either crafted or uncrafted, the meaning is that even if a bodhisattva’s continuum is thoroughly imbued with faith, if they lack innate wisdom, they will quickly fall away from attaining perfect enlightenment. However, if that same faithful one possesses the realization of the supreme perfection of wisdom, and is neither tainted by the afflictive obscurations due to being inferior, nor impaired by the cognitive obscurations due to arrogance, they will touch and attain the enlightenment of the Victorious One.

heading: **རྒད་པོ་འདོད་པ་བརྟན་མི་ཡོད་པ་དང་མེད་པའི་དཔེ།**
translation: Thus it is said. From "having reached one hundred and twenty years" up to "will touch," regarding the analogy of the old man, the meaning is that even if a bodhisattva who possesses only a weak power of wisdom that realizes selflessness has initially entered the path through faith, they will quickly decline in the interim. However, if that same faithful one is completely seized by both the method of great compassion and the supreme wisdom that knows non-apprehension, they will not decline due to adverse conditions in the interim, and they will touch the enlightenment of the Tathāgatas.

From "Why is that?" up to "Thus it is said," the reason is that the qualities of a learned teacher arise from the student relying upon them, and because the learned one is the instructor who teaches the perfection of wisdom to those students. Therefore, because the Conquerors, who possess the supreme of all virtues, have said that the path of the Buddha and the resultant phenomena depend upon an authentic spiritual friend, it is said thus.

heading: **དེ་ཉེ་བར་སྟོན་པའི་དོན།**
translation: Thus it is said. From "generosity and ethical discipline" up to "should be taught in this way," although the context of the three knowledges teaches the manifestation of wisdom, for those who are beginners, it is taught starting with generosity. As for how generosity is of three types, having given whatever gift one may have, one should dedicate it to enlightenment; the supreme enlightenment is such that the one who dedicates, the object of dedication, and the dedication itself are all exhausted and unapprehended, and one should dedicate by sealing it with the wisdom that knows the nature of the non-existence of truth in all that is to be dedicated and the one who dedicates. The "possessing the six" has been explained above. Likewise, one should dedicate all roots of virtue that have become enlightenment through ethical discipline, patience, diligence, concentration, and wisdom toward enlightenment, and one should teach the beginner in this way: "Do not grasp at that enlightenment, which is to be attained as the ultimate reality, as a supreme object of attachment to the aggregates and so forth."

heading: **འགྲོ་བ་ལ་བྱེད་པ་དུ་མའི་སྦྱོར་བ་དང་ལྡན་པ།**
translation: Up to the point of saying "is unperturbed," those who are like a lake that is clear and cool because of such practice, and who are as full as the moon among those who speak, are protectors because they save beings from suffering and place them in happiness; they are a refuge because they remove the causes of suffering; they are a support because they proceed toward enlightenment; they are an eye because they realize it; they are an intellect, an island, and a guide because they desire to perform the benefit of others; they are a lamp because they clarify through selflessness and remove ignorance; and they are supreme because they enter into all vehicles of the Dharma, and they are unperturbed in their speech.

Thus it is said. From "generosity and ethical discipline" up to "should be taught in this way," although the context of the three knowledges teaches the manifestation of wisdom, for those who are beginners, it is taught starting with generosity. As for how generosity is of three types, having given whatever gift one may have, one should dedicate it to enlightenment; the supreme enlightenment is such that the one who dedicates, the object of dedication, and the dedication itself are all exhausted and unapprehended, and one should dedicate by sealing it with the wisdom that knows the nature of the non-existence of truth in all that is to be dedicated and the one who dedicates. The "possessing the six" has been explained above. Likewise, one should dedicate all roots of virtue that have become enlightenment through ethical discipline, patience, diligence, concentration, and wisdom toward enlightenment, and one should teach the beginner in this way: "Do not grasp at that enlightenment, which is to be attained as the ultimate reality, as a supreme object of attachment to the aggregates and so forth."

heading: **ཆོས་ཟབ་མོ་ངེས་པ།**
translation: Thus it is said, from "those such as these" up to "should be known." Those bodhisattvas possess such qualities of being irreversible in their signs, and their minds are free from the conceptual proliferation of objects. In this way, they are free from hesitation, doubt, and uncertainty regarding the meaning of suchness, and they possess the meaning of the abiding nature. Having heard the Mother, the perfection of wisdom, they have given rise to definitive understanding, and thus their minds do not waver. They do not rely upon others, and one should know them to be great bodhisattvas who are irreversible.

translation:
From "of the guides" up to "made little concern," this Dharma that the guides, the Buddhas, have realized is by nature profound, because it is difficult to see and difficult to understand. Previously, for those who had no realization at the time of the cause and would not attain it at the time of the result, the Victorious One, who long benefited sentient beings and was immediately possessed of compassion, having attained enlightenment himself, thought, "Even if I teach this that I have attained to others, they will not perceive it as a gathering of sentient beings." As it is said:

"I have realized a Dharma that is profound, free from proliferation, luminous, and unconditioned,
Like nectar.
Since no one to whom I might teach it would understand,
I shall remain silent and dwell in the forest."

Having said this, he made little concern.

Thus it is said, from "those such as these" up to "should be known." Those bodhisattvas possess such qualities of being irreversible in their signs, and their minds are free from the conceptual proliferation of objects. In this way, they are free from hesitation, doubt, and uncertainty regarding the meaning of suchness, and they possess the meaning of the abiding nature. Having heard the Mother, the perfection of wisdom, they have given rise to definitive understanding, and thus their minds do not waver. They do not rely upon others, and one should know them to be great bodhisattvas who are irreversible.

heading: **དངོས།**
translation: From "the space element" up to "there is no distinction," how is it that these things do not exist in phenomena? The space element is limitless in the eastern direction, the southern direction, and likewise in the western direction and the northern direction. Even though it exists in the upward direction, the downward direction, and in all ten directions, there is no variation in form among these, nor is there any distinction in their characteristics. Just as in that example, the suchness of past Buddhas, the wisdom of future Buddhas, and the suchness of present Buddhas are all the same suchness. Whatever is the suchness of the present is also the suchness of the Arhats, and it is the suchness of all phenomena of the afflicted cycle of existence and the suchness of all phenomena of the purified state of nirvana. Whatever is the suchness of all of these is the suchness of the Victorious Ones; therefore, in this suchness of all phenomena, there is no distinction of good, bad, or the like.

From "the space element" up to "there is no distinction," how is it that these things do not exist in phenomena? The space element is limitless in the eastern direction, the southern direction, and likewise in the western direction and the northern direction. Even though it exists in the upward direction, the downward direction, and in all ten directions, there is no variation in form among these, nor is there any distinction in their characteristics. Just as in that example, the suchness of past Buddhas, the wisdom of future Buddhas, and the suchness of present Buddhas are all the same suchness. Whatever is the suchness of the present is also the suchness of the Arhats, and it is the suchness of all phenomena of the afflicted cycle of existence and the suchness of all phenomena of the purified state of nirvana. Whatever is the suchness of all of these is the suchness of the Victorious Ones; therefore, in this suchness of all phenomena, there is no distinction of good, bad, or the like.

heading: **དེས་བཟློག་པ།**
translation: So it is said: from "the wisdom of the guide" up to "falling into the state of a śrāvaka," if one has compassion but lacks the wisdom that knows the guide as unapprehendable, one will not attain awakening. Just as in the example of grasping at the extreme of permanence, these five perfections—the path of the Victors, such as the perfection of generosity—even if practiced constantly for a long time over countless eons, and even if one has made vast and infinite prayers for their expansion and has constantly relied upon the path in the world, if one lacks the means of great compassion and is not joined with the knowledge that wisdom is unapprehendable, one falls into the state of a śrāvaka.

heading: **དྲི་བ་དང་ལན་གྱི་ཞུགས་པའི་ཕྱིར་མི་ལྡོག་པའི་རྟགས།**
translation: So it is said: from "to the Protector of the World" up to "please grant the prophecy," the noble elder Subhūti, because he is abiding on the path of preparation, fully requests the signs of irreversibility. These qualities are like an ocean, and he requests that the Buddha reveal the signs by which those inexhaustible bodhisattvas do not turn back to the inferior vehicle, which is devoid of afflictions. He requests that the Victorious One prophesy certain of these qualities, such as how they possess great power in working for the benefit of others and the manner in which they are truthful, so that they do not turn back from the mind of the Great Vehicle.

source: ཅེས་གསུངས་ཏེ། ཐ་དད་འདུ་ཤེས་ཞེས་པ་ནས། གཞན་གྱི་དྲིང་མི་འཇོག་ཅེས་པའི་བར་ལ། ལན་བཀའ་བསྩལ་པ་དང༌། འཁོར་འདས་ཐ་དད་དུ་བདེན་པའི་འདུ་ཤེས་དང་བྲལ་ཞིང་རིགས་དང་ལྡན་པའི་བདེན་པའི་ཚིག་སྨྲ་བ་དང༌། ཕྱི་རོལ་པའི་དགེ་སྦྱོང་དག་དང་བྲམ་ཟེ་གཞན་ལ་སྐྱབས་གནས་སུ་བརྟེན་པ་མི་བྱེད། རྒྱུ་འབྲས་ལ་མཁས་པས་དུས་རྣམས་རྟག་ཏུ་རྒྱུ་མི་དགེ་བ་སྤངས་པས་འབྲས་བུ་ངན་སོང་གསུམ་པོ་ཡང་སྤངས་ཏེ། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་དེ་དག་དགེ་བ་བཅུའི་ལས་ཀྱི་ལམ་ཉམས་སུ་ལེན་པ་ལ། མངོན་པར་བརྩོན་ཞིང་ཟང་ཟིང་དང་བསྙེན་བཀུར་དང་སྙན་གྲགས་ལ་བལྟ་བའི་སེམས་མེད་པར་འགྲོ་བ་ལ་ཆོས་ནི་རྗེས་སུ་སྟོན་པ་དང༌། སྤྱི་དང་ཁྱད་པར་དུ་ཐེག་ཆེན་ཆོས་ལ་གཅིག་ཏུ་དགའ་ཞིང་ཐེ་ཚོམ་མེད་པ་དང༌། དུས་རྟག་ཏུ་ཚིག་འཇམ་པ་དང༌། ངེས་པ་དང་ལྡན་ཞིང༌། འགྲོ་བ་དང༌། འཆག་པ་དང༌། ཉལ་བ་དང༌། འདུག་པ་སྟེ་སྤྱོད་ལམ་རྣམ་པ་བཞིར་ཤེས་བཞིན་དང་རབ་ཏུ་ལྡན་ན། དེའི་དབང་གི་འགྲོ་ན་མིག་གཉའ་ཤིང་ཙམ་དུ་དྲང་པོར་བལྟ་ཞིང་འགྲོ་བ་ལ་སྤྱོད་ལམ་ཐ་དད་ཀྱི་སེམས་འཁྲུལ་པ་མེད་པ་དང༌། རྒྱུད་ལ་སྒྲིབ་པ་ལྔའི་དྲི་མ་མེད་པས་གཙང་བར་བྱས་ཤིང་གཙང་མའི་གོས་སྣམ་སྦྱར་བླ་གོས་ཐང་གོས་གསུམ་འཆང་ཞིང་གསུམ་པོ་ལ་ཤིག་སྲོའམ་ཁ་ན་མ་ཐོ་བས་དབེན་ཞིང་དག་པ་དང༌། སྦྱངས་པའི་ཡོན་ཏན་ལ་བསྟེན་པས་རྙེད་པ་འདོད་པ་མ་ཡིན་ཞིང་མིའི་ཁྱུ་མཆོག་ཏུ་གྱུར་པས་དུས་རྟག་ཏུ་ཐེག་ཆེན་གྱི་ཆོས་འདོད་པ་དང༌། དམན་པ་དང་རློམ་པའི་བདུད་ཀྱི་ཡུལ་ལས་འདས་ཤིང་འདྲེན་པ་གཞན་གྱི་དྲིང་ལ་མི་འཇོག་པ་སྟེ། བཅུ་དྲུག་པོ་སྦྱོར་ལམ་ལ་གནས་པའི་ཕྱིར་མི་ལྡོག་པའི་རྟགས་ཡིན་ནོ། །
translation: So it is said: from "the recognition of difference" up to "not relying on others," the response is given. Being free from the recognition that saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are truly different, they speak words of truth that are consistent with their lineage, and they do not rely upon other non-Buddhist ascetics or brahmins as their refuge. Being skilled in cause and effect, they always abandon non-virtuous causes, and thus they also abandon the three lower realms as their result. Those bodhisattvas, while practicing the path of the ten virtuous actions, strive diligently and, without a mind that looks toward material gain, veneration, or fame, they teach the Dharma to beings. They are singularly joyful and free from doubt regarding the Dharma of the Great Vehicle in general and in particular. They are always gentle in speech, possess certainty, and are well-endowed with mindfulness in the four modes of deportment: walking, standing, lying down, and sitting. By the power of this, when they walk, they look straight ahead for the distance of a yoke, and they have no confused mind regarding their various modes of deportment. Their continuum is purified, being free from the stains of the five obscurations, and they wear the three robes—the inner, upper, and outer—which are clean, free from lice, nits, or faults. By relying on the qualities of asceticism, they do not desire gain, and having become the best of men, they always desire the Dharma of the Great Vehicle. They transcend the domain of the māras of inferiority and arrogance, and they do not rely on other guides. These sixteen are the signs of irreversibility for one abiding on the path of preparation.

So it is said: from "the Buddha vehicle" up to "should speak," one who relies upon this Great Vehicle, the Buddha vehicle, and wishes to definitively emerge from the extremes of existence and peace, should train with an even mind toward all beings, without partiality, having the recognition of them as parents and so forth. They should train with a mind that seeks the long-term benefit of sentient beings and a mind of loving-kindness that provides immediate happiness. Furthermore, they should be free from the malice of harmful intent, and, being free from deceit and guile, they should speak gentle words that are upright, pleasant to the ear, and delightful to the mind.

So it is said: from "to the Protector of the World" up to "please grant the prophecy," the noble elder Subhūti, because he is abiding on the path of preparation, fully requests the signs of irreversibility. These qualities are like an ocean, and he requests that the Buddha reveal the signs by which those inexhaustible bodhisattvas do not turn back to the inferior vehicle, which is devoid of afflictions. He requests that the Victorious One prophesy certain of these qualities, such as how they possess great power in working for the benefit of others and the manner in which they are truthful, so that they do not turn back from the mind of the Great Vehicle.

heading: **དྲི་བ་དང་ལན་གྱི་ཞུགས་པའི་ཕྱིར་མི་ལྡོག་པའི་རྟགས།**
source: ཞེས་གསུངས་ཏེ། བསམ་གཏན་བཞི་ལ་ཞེས་པ་ནས། འདི་དག་ཡིན་པར་ཤེས་པར་བྱ་ཞེས་པའི་བར་ལ། བསམ་གཏན་བཞི་ལ་སེམས་གནས་ཀྱང་བསམ་གཏན་དེར་དྲོད་མྱང་བའི་ཚུལ་གྱིས་མི་གནས་པ་དང༌། སྒྲ་ཐམས་ཅད་བྲག་ཆར་རྟོགས་པས་སྙན་པ་དང་གྲགས་པ་འདོད་པ་མ་ཡིན་ཞིང༌། རྒྱུད་ཁོང་ཁྲོ་བས་སེམས་ལ་དཀྲིས་ཤིང་བཅིངས་པ་མེད་པ་དང༌། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གཞན་དོན་དུ་ཁྱིམ་པར་འགྱུར་ནའང༌། དུས་རྟག་ཏུ་འདོད་ཡོན་བསྟེན་ཀྱང་འདོད་ཡོན་གྱི་དངོས་པོ་ཀུན་ལ་ཞེན་པས་མ་ཆགས་པ་དང༌། སྲོག་འཚོ་བའི་ཕྱིར་ནི་རྐུ་བ་དང་བསོད་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་སྤང་བ་དང་བཅས་པས་ལོངས་སྤྱོད་འཚོ་བར་མི་བྱེད་པ་དང༌། བརྡེག་རྩོག་ལ་སོགས་པ་དྲག་ཤུལ་སྤྱོད་པ་དང༌། གནོད་འགྱུར་གྱི་སྔགས་བཟླས་པར་མི་བྱེད་པ་དང༌། བུད་མེད་དབང་བསྡུད་སྦྱོར་སྔགས་བྱེད་པ་མིན་པ་དང༌། བསྙེན་བཀུར་འདོད་པའི་ལས་ཅན་བུ་བཙའ་བ་དང་བུ་མོ་བཙའ་བར་འགྱུར་རོ། །ཞེས་ཕོ་མོར་གྱུར་ཞེས་ལུང་སྟོན་པར་མི་བྱེད་དེ། ཤཱ་རིའི་བུས་ཁྱིམ་བདག་ལུང་བསྟན་པ་ལྟ་བུའོ། །ཕུང་པོ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་གཏམ་གྱི་སྦྱོར་བ་རྗེས་སུ་སྦྱོར་བས་རབ་ཏུ་དབེན་པའི་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་མཆོག་ལ་བརྩོན་པ་དང༌། ལུས་ཀྱི་སྒོ་ནས་འཐབ་པ་དང༌། ངག་གི་སྒོ་ནས་རྩོད་པ་དང་བྲལ་ཞིང་བདེ་བ་དང་ཕྲད་པར་འདོད་པའི་བྱམས་པའི་སེམས་ཀྱང་བསྟན་པ་དང༌། དུས་ཐམས་ཅད་དུ་ཀུན་མཁྱེན་ཐོབ་པར་འདོད་ཅིང་བསྟན་པའི་བསླབ་པ་གསུམ་ལ་རྟག་ཏུ་གཞོལ་བའི་སེམས་དང་ལྡན་པ་དང༌། སྐྱེ་བ་ལ་དབང་ཐོབ་པས་ཡུལ་མཐའ་འཁོབ་དང༌། མི་ཀླ་ཀློ་སྐྱེ་བོའི་ཡུལ་གྱི་མཐའ་སྐྱེ་བ་རྣམ་པར་སྤངས་པ་དང༌། ཕྱིར་མི་ལྡོག་པའི་རྟགས་མཐོང་བས་རང་གི་ས་ལ་དོགས་པ་མེད་པའི་རྟོགས་པ་བརྟན་པོས་རྟག་ཏུ་རི་རབ་དང་འདྲ་བ་དང༌། ཆོས་འཚོལ་བ་ལ་ངོམས་པ་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་སྲོག་ཀྱང་འདོར་ཕོད་པའི་ནུས་པ་དང་ལྡན་ཞིང༌། ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ཉམས་སུ་ལེན་པའི་རྣལ་འབྱོར་པ་ལ་རབ་ཏུ་བརྩོན་པས་སྟེ་བཅུ་དྲུག་པོ་དེ། མཐོང་ལམ་ཕྱིར་མི་ལྡོག་པའི་རྟགས་ནི་འདི་དག་ཡིན་པར་ཤེས་པར་བྱའོ། །
translation: It is said: from the phrase "in the four concentrations" up to the phrase "one should know these to be the case," [the meaning is as follows]: although the mind abides in the four concentrations, one does not abide in those concentrations in a manner that experiences their warmth; because one understands all sounds to be like echoes, one does not desire praise or fame; because the mental continuum is not bound or tied by the mind of anger, there is no [affliction]; even if a bodhisattva becomes a householder for the sake of others, although they always utilize the objects of desire, they are not attached to them because they do not crave any of the substances of desire; for the sake of sustaining life, they do not live by means of wealth that involves abandoning [virtue] such as stealing or begging; they do not engage in violent conduct such as striking or fighting; they do not recite mantras that cause harm; they do not perform mantras for the purpose of subjugating women; and they do not predict that those who desire to be served will give birth to sons or daughters—they do not make such predictions of becoming male or female, just as Subhūti did not make a prediction for the householder. They strive for the supreme perfection of wisdom, which is thoroughly isolated by engaging in the discourse of the aggregates and so forth; they show a mind of loving-kindness that desires to meet with happiness, while being free from fighting through the body and arguing through speech; they possess a mind that is always devoted to the three trainings, desiring to attain omniscience at all times; because they have attained mastery over birth, they have completely abandoned birth in borderlands and in the lands of uncivilized peoples; by seeing the signs of non-retrogression, they are always like Mount Meru, with firm realization and without doubt regarding their own stage; because they are insatiable in their search for the Dharma, they possess the power to dare to cast away even their lives; and by being thoroughly diligent as a yogi who practices the perfection of wisdom—these sixteen are to be known as the signs of non-retrogression on the path of seeing.

heading: **དེ་རྟོགས་པའི་བསོད་ནམས།**
translation: From "Bodhisattva" up to "will attain," the merit of a Bodhisattva who realizes this is as follows: for any Bodhisattva who has realized this profound way, and who has realized this Dharma—which is the path of the cause, the ultimate, non-attached, emptiness, and in which there is not even the existence of phenomena included within the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields—what other merit could be greater than the perfect merit generated in even a single day? There is none. If one asks how much merit is attained by this: for example, if a lustful person who engages in the objects of desire were to make an appointment with a woman, but because someone else took her away, he did not meet her, then the number of moments of discursive thought in his mind during that one day—the merit generated by taking that number as the count of eons—is the amount of merit that the Bodhisattva will attain.

From "Bodhisattva" up to "will attain," the merit of a Bodhisattva who realizes this is as follows: for any Bodhisattva who has realized this profound way, and who has realized this Dharma—which is the path of the cause, the ultimate, non-attached, emptiness, and in which there is not even the existence of phenomena included within the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields—what other merit could be greater than the perfect merit generated in even a single day? There is none. If one asks how much merit is attained by this: for example, if a lustful person who engages in the objects of desire were to make an appointment with a woman, but because someone else took her away, he did not meet her, then the number of moments of discursive thought in his mind during that one day—the merit generated by taking that number as the count of eons—is the amount of merit that the Bodhisattva will attain.

heading: **དེ་བསྒོམ་པའི་བསོད་ནམས།**
translation: Thus it is said. From "Bodhisattva" up to "does not exist in the three [worlds]," the meaning is as follows: if any Bodhisattva meditates in meditative equipoise upon that previously taught meaning, the supreme meaning of the perfection of wisdom, and then, having arisen from that meditative equipoise, teaches the Dharma to others while remaining untainted by the three faults of conceptual focus, discursive thought, and attachment and aversion, and if they also dedicate that merit of teaching as a cause of awakening for the sake of beings, then what need is there to speak of anything superior to that virtue? Indeed, there is nothing in the three worlds—above the earth, below the earth, or upon the earth—that is equal to it.

translation: Thus it is said. From "that merit is also" up to "fully embraces," the meaning is as follows: one should know that such merit is like an accumulation because it lacks a core of truth; likewise, it is empty because it lacks an intrinsic nature, it is like a hollow shell because it is a mere reflection, it is like a fabrication because it is artificial, and it is without essence because its result lacks truth. When one practices the perfection of wisdom of the Sugatas in this way, even while practicing, one fully embraces an immeasurable number of merits.

heading: **ལམ་གྱི་རང་བཞིན་མེད་ཀྱི་ཆོས་ཉིད་ཀྱི་འཕེལ་བ།**
translation: From "taught by the Buddha" up to "will attain the supreme," the meaning is as follows: If one asks, "If the reality of phenomena (dharmatā) is without increase or decrease, then it is illogical that merit should increase through meditation," [the answer is that] the attainment of awakening through the purification of adventitious stains upon that which is naturally pure is taught only as a summary in the Buddha's sutras; it will be explained in detail through the obstacles and the means of accomplishment. Having understood that all these enumerations of phenomena are merely verbal expressions and mere conventions, and that they lack any intrinsic nature, even though one may have practiced accumulation and purification for many tens of millions of eons and spoken of many increases and decreases, because the expanse of phenomena (dharmadhātu) is primordially without fault, there is no immediate exhaustion, and because its qualities are primordially perfect, there is no immediate increase. Having understood that those six phenomena called the perfections of the Victors are also proclaimed only as mere names and mere symbols, that Bodhisattva who dedicates such merit—which is merely a name—to awakening, and who is free from the pride of grasping at truth, does not suffer any decline in the reality of phenomena and will attain the supreme awakening of a Buddha as their fruit.

source: ཞེས་གསུངས་ཏེ། འབྲུ་མར་སྙིང་པོ་ཞེས་པ་ནས། སངས་རྒྱས་འགྱུར་ཞེས་པའི་བར་ལ། དེ་ལྟར་ནའམ། ཀུན་རྫོབ་ཏུ་སེམས་བསྐྱེད་པ་དང་པོ་དང་ཐ་མ་འཚོགས་པ་མེད་པས་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཐོབ་པར་མི་འཐད་དོ་ཞེ་ན། མ་འཚོགས་ཀྱང་ཐོབ་པའི་དཔེ་ནི། འབྲུ་མར་དང་སྡོང་བུ་ཡིས་བསྟན་ཏེ། དེ་བཞིན་དུ་ལས་དང་པོ་པའི་དུས་ན་འདུན་པ་དང་ལྡན་པའི་སེམས་ཀྱི་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཀྱི་མཆོག་ལ་རེག་པར་ནུས་པ་མ་ཡིན་ལ། དེ་མེད་པར་ཡང་བྱང་ཆུབ་དེ་ལ་རེག་པར་ནུས་པ་མ་ཡིན་ལ། ཡང་ཐ་མ་རྡོ་རྗེ་ལྟ་བུའི་སེམས་ཀྱིས་ཀྱང་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཞི་བ་ཐོབ་མིན་ལ། དེ་མེད་པར་ཡང་བྱང་ཆུབ་དེ་ཐོབ་པར་ནུས་པ་མ་ཡིན་ནོ།། ཡང་དེ་ལ་འབྲས་བུ་འབྱིན་པའི་ཚེ་ན་སྔར་གྱི་རྒྱུ་ས་བོན་བཏབ་པ་ལས་ནི་འབྲས་བུ་མྱུ་གུ་དང་མེ་ཏོག་དང་འབྲས་བུ་འབྱུང་བར་འགྱུར་ལ། དེ་ཡང་ས་བོན་ལ་སོགས་རིམ་གྱིས་འགག་ཀྱང་ནུས་པ་ཡར་ལྡན་དུ་དགོས་པས་ཤིང་ཡང་མེད་པ་དེ་མིན་པ་ལྟར། དཔེ་དེ་བཞིན་དུ་དང་པོ་འདུན་པ་དང་ལྡན་པའི་སེམས་ཀྱང་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱུ་ཡིན་ཏེ། དེའི་ངོ་བོ་འགགས་ཀྱང་ནུས་པར་ལྡན་དུ་རྡོ་རྗེ་ལྟ་བུའི་བར་དུ་བསྒོམས་པས་བྱང་ཆུབ་མེད་པ་སྟེ་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །ཡང་བྱང་ཆུབ་ལ་སྦྱོར་བ་ལས་བཅུའི་གྲངས་དང་གོ་རིམ་ལ་ལྟོས་པའི་དཔེ་ནི་དཔེར་ན་ཆུའི་ཐིགས་པ་དང་པོ་དང་ཐ་མའི་བར་དུ་རིམ་གྱིས་ཉུང་ངུ་ཉུང་ངུ་བླུགས་པས་བུམ་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་འགེངས་པ་ལྟར་དུ། དཔེ་དེ་བཞིན་དུ་དང་པོ་འདུན་པ་དང་ལྡན་པའི་སེམས་ཀྱང་བྱང་ཆུབ་མཆོག་གི་རྒྱུ་ཡིན་ཏེ། ཐ་མའི་སེམས་ཀྱང་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཀྱི་རྒྱུ་ཡིན་པས། རིམ་གྱིས་རིམ་གྱིས་དཀར་པོའི་ཡོན་ཏན་རྫོགས་པའི་སངས་རྒྱས་སུ་འགྱུར་རོ། །
translation: Thus it is said. From "the essence of oil and wick" up to "will become a Buddha," the meaning is as follows: If one asks, "If that is so, or if, conventionally, the initial and final generation of the mind do not meet, then it is illogical that awakening should be attained," the example for attaining it even without meeting is shown by the oil and the wick. In the same way, at the time of a beginner, the mind endowed with aspiration is not able to touch supreme awakening, yet without it, one is also not able to touch that awakening; and again, the final diamond-like mind does not attain peaceful awakening, yet without it, one is also not able to attain that awakening. Furthermore, at the time of producing the fruit, from the previously planted causal seed, the fruit—the sprout, the flower, and the result—arises; and although the seed and so forth cease in sequence, because the capacity must be possessed in succession, it is not the case that the tree does not exist. Just like that example, the mind of the beginner endowed with aspiration is also a cause of awakening; because one meditates until the diamond-like mind, possessing the capacity even though its essence has ceased, it is not the case that awakening does not exist. Furthermore, the example regarding the number and sequence of the ten [stages] of engagement in awakening is like a water vessel being completely filled by pouring in small amounts, drop by drop, from the first to the last. Just like that example, the mind of the beginner endowed with aspiration is a cause of supreme awakening, and the final mind is also a cause of awakening; therefore, by degrees, one becomes a Buddha whose white qualities are perfected.

[2-170] translation already produced for this document:
From "taught by the Buddha" up to "will attain the supreme," the meaning is as follows: If one asks, "If the reality of phenomena (dharmatā) is without increase or decrease, then it is illogical that merit should increase through meditation," [the answer is that] the attainment of awakening through the purification of adventitious stains upon that which is naturally pure is taught only as a summary in the Buddha's sutras; it will be explained in detail through the obstacles and the means of accomplishment. Having understood that all these enumerations of phenomena are merely verbal expressions and mere conventions, and that they lack any intrinsic nature, even though one may have practiced accumulation and purification for many tens of millions of eons and spoken of many increases and decreases, because the expanse of phenomena (dharmadhātu) is primordially without fault, there is no immediate exhaustion, and because its qualities are primordially perfect, there is no immediate increase. Having understood that those six phenomena called the perfections of the Victors are also proclaimed only as mere names and mere symbols, that Bodhisattva who dedicates such merit—which is merely a name—to awakening, and who is free from the pride of grasping at truth, does not suffer any decline in the reality of phenomena and will attain the supreme awakening of a Buddha as their fruit.

heading: **ལམ་མཐའ་གཉིས་དང་བྲལ་བ།**
translation: From "empty and signless" up to "like that which does not abide": possessing both profundity and vastness means practicing the dharma by way of emptiness, which is empty by nature regarding all phenomena of the afflicted samsaric realm and the purified nirvanic realm; by way of signlessness, which is empty by cause; and by way of wishlessness, which is empty by result. Furthermore, not even touching upon the mere emptiness of nirvana, and not practicing even worldly signs, one does not abide in the extremes of existence or peace, just like the example of the dangerous place.

translation: It is said: From "practicing in this way" up to "is practicing the perfection of wisdom," it means that a bodhisattva practicing in this way has no conceit, thinking, "Even if I am prophesied by a buddha endowed with the ten powers, just as a śrāvaka is, I will attain enlightenment." Furthermore, because they think, "There is no cause whatsoever for attaining this enlightenment, the dharmakāya," they have no fear of enlightenment. Thus, practicing in this way is practicing the wisdom of the sugatas.

heading: **སྒྱུ་མ་ཤེས་པའི་དཔེས་སེམས་ཅན་མི་འདོར་བ།**
translation: From "like a person" up to "does not touch," it means that just as in the example of knowing a magical illusion, at the time when one connects skillful means with wisdom, a bodhisattva who possesses skillful means also generates great compassion for the realms of sentient beings in this very life. They transcend the fear of falling into the two stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, as well as the four māras, such as one's own aggregates. They abide in the supreme meditative concentration of the three gateways to liberation, and unlike the śrāvakas, they do not touch the peaceful enlightenment, but rather, in accordance with the Great Vehicle, they strive for the benefit of beings and will attain enlightenment.

heading: **འཇིག་རྟེན་ལ་སོགས་པའི་དཔེས་སྨོན་པ་མི་འདོར་བ།**
translation: Thus it is said: From "relying on the wind in the sky" up to "practicing supreme peace in peace," it means that just as in the example of the world coming into being through karma, the mind that rests in the emptiness of the nature of reality, which is like the sky, relies on the aspiration to ripen beings in conventional reality when it knows the nature of sentient beings. It demonstrates many various activities of benefit and happiness, yet it does not touch nirvana, and it does not have a mind that rests by relying on emptiness. At whatever time a bodhisattva, having the remainder of their training, is wise and clear through realizing the meaning, they practice this supreme meditative concentration of the peace of the emptiness of the nature of reality; during that interval, they do not intensely meditate on signs or objects of observation. Because they dwell without the signs of the emptiness of causes and have no aspirations for the emptiness of results, they practice supreme peace in peace.

From "like a person" up to "does not touch," it means that just as in the example of knowing a magical illusion, at the time when one connects skillful means with wisdom, a bodhisattva who possesses skillful means also generates great compassion for the realms of sentient beings in this very life. They transcend the fear of falling into the two stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, as well as the four māras, such as one's own aggregates. They abide in the supreme meditative concentration of the three gateways to liberation, and unlike the śrāvakas, they do not touch the peaceful enlightenment, but rather, in accordance with the Great Vehicle, they strive for the benefit of beings and will attain enlightenment.

heading: **བྱའི་དཔེས་གནས་མེད་ཀྱང་མི་ལྷུང་བ།**
translation: Thus it is said: From "flying in the sky" up to "not practicing," it means that just as in the example of a bird flying in the sky not falling to the ground, that bodhisattva, who is like a bird, practices the emptiness that is the door to liberation, which is like the sky. Because they possess the skillful means of great compassion, they do not touch nirvana, and because they realize that there is no intrinsic nature, they do not practice upon signs.

Thus it is said: From "relying on the wind in the sky" up to "practicing supreme peace in peace," it means that just as in the example of the world coming into being through karma, the mind that rests in the emptiness of the nature of reality, which is like the sky, relies on the aspiration to ripen beings in conventional reality when it knows the nature of sentient beings. It demonstrates many various activities of benefit and happiness, yet it does not touch nirvana, and it does not have a mind that rests by relying on emptiness. At whatever time a bodhisattva, having the remainder of their training, is wise and clear through realizing the meaning, they practice this supreme meditative concentration of the peace of the emptiness of the nature of reality; during that interval, they do not intensely meditate on signs or objects of observation. Because they dwell without the signs of the emptiness of causes and have no aspirations for the emptiness of results, they practice supreme peace in peace.

heading: **མདའི་དཔེ་དགེ་བ་མ་རྫོགས་པའི་བར་དུ་སྟོང་ཉིད་མངོན་གསུམ་དུ་མི་བྱེད་པ།**
translation: Thus it is said: From "just as a person trained in archery" up to "that supreme one is not attained," it means that, following the example of the arrow, the bodhisattva who practices the supreme perfection of wisdom—the path—possesses the distinct qualities of wisdom, skillful means, power, and miraculous ability. By these, they practice in the state of having no intrinsic nature. As long as the roots of virtue that make one a buddha are not perfected, they do not attain that supreme emptiness which is pervasive and connected with great compassion.

heading: **རྫུ་འཕྲུལ་གྱི་དཔེས་འཁོར་བར་གནས་ཀྱང་མི་སྐྱེ་བ།**
translation: Thus it is said: From "just as a monk" up to "no exhaustion," it means that, following the example of the monk, the wise bodhisattva abides in the emptiness of the nature of phenomena, which is like the sky. Yet, even though they remain in the cycle of existence for ten million eons, they feel no weariness in their mind and have no exhaustion in their body.

heading: **གདུགས་ཀྱི་དཔེས་ལམ་མཐའ་གཉིས་སུ་མི་ལྟུང་བ།**
translation: Thus it is said: From "just as a person" up to "also sees the phenomena," it means that, following the example of a person holding a parasol, the wise bodhisattva who possesses the bodhicitta and abides in great compassion holds up two parasols by means of the two: skillful means, which is great compassion, and wisdom, which is the knowledge of non-observation. What are these? Through wisdom, they contemplate the phenomena of the afflictions of cyclic existence and the phenomena of purification as being emptiness, which is empty of their own intrinsic nature, as the signlessness of being empty of causes, and as the wishlessness of being empty of results. Through skillful means, which is great compassion, they do not touch upon nirvana, and they also see the suchness of all phenomena.

Thus it is said: From "just as a person" up to "also sees the phenomena," it means that, following the example of a person holding a parasol, the wise bodhisattva who possesses the bodhicitta and abides in great compassion holds up two parasols by means of the two: skillful means, which is great compassion, and wisdom, which is the knowledge of non-observation. What are these? Through wisdom, they contemplate the phenomena of the afflictions of cyclic existence and the phenomena of purification as being emptiness, which is empty of their own intrinsic nature, as the signlessness of being empty of causes, and as the wishlessness of being empty of results. Through skillful means, which is great compassion, they do not touch upon nirvana, and they also see the suchness of all phenomena.

heading: **ཚོང་པའི་དཔེས་ལམ་མཐའ་གཉིས་ལ་འདྲིས་པ།**
translation: Thus it is said: From "seeking the goal" up to "knowing the method," it means that, following the example of the merchant, the bodhisattva, whose skill in means and wisdom is clear, becomes proficient in all the wisdom of realization and the liberation of abandonment of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, who are like an intermediate town. Yet, they do not abide there by way of tasting its flavor; nor do they abide in the buddha-wisdom, which is like the jewel island; nor do they abide in the unconditioned characteristic, which is like their own home. Nevertheless, they are those who know the method of the path that is appropriate for each.

heading: **རྒྱུ་འབྲས་གཉིས་ཀའི་སྒོ་ནས་མཇུག་བསྡུ་བ།**
translation: Thus it is said: From "whenever there is love for beings" up to "there is no abode," it means that whenever a bodhisattva, having continuously connected with great love for sentient beings, engages in the meditative concentrations of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, they will attain the peace of nirvana, being free from the two extremes. The assertion that "they abide in peace or in the unconditioned of existence" is a state that has no basis and no occasion.

heading: **ལུང་མ་བསྟན་པ།**
translation: Thus it is said: From "if the practice" up to "should be known," it means that if others ask, "What are the practices, faculties, and signs of one who is irreversible?" and that bodhisattva does not reveal their own experience, nor the dharmas of emptiness and signlessness, and even when asked about the dharmas of the signs of irreversibility, does not explain them, it should be known that this is what the Buddha previously did not predict. With this, the complete explanation of the aspects of full awakening is finished.

heading: **ལུང་མ་བསྟན་པ།**
translation:
The essence of the peak clear realization of the fifth chapter is the attainment of a spontaneously present intellect that realizes, without effort, the non-apprehension of the three paths that are the causes of the dharmakāya. Regarding this, it is said:

"Its signs and the increase of aspects,
Stability and the abiding of the entire mind,
What is called 'seeing' and 'meditation,'
The paths of activity are distinct;
The four antidotes to the four types
Of conceptualization, along with
The uninterrupted meditative concentration
And the erroneous practice,
Are the peak clear realization
From which the fruit of true awakening arises."

Thus, it is taught through eight divisions from the perspective of generating these qualities within the continuum.

heading: **ལུང་བསྟན་ཐོབ་པ།**
translation: Thus it is said: From "Arhat" up to "should be known," it means that one does not desire, even in a dream, the level of an Arhat of the Lesser Vehicle, the wisdom of a Pratyekabuddha, or the splendor of the three realms; and if one sees in a dream that one sees the Buddhas, that they are seated on thrones, and that they are teaching the Dharma to sentient beings, it should be known that this is one who has been prophesied as irreversible from before.

ཞེས་གསུངས་ཏེ།
[2-189] translation already produced for this document:
Thus it is said:

[2-190] source:
གལ་ཏེ་སྤྱོད་པ་དང་ནི་ཞེས་པ་ནས། རིག་པར་བྱ་ཞེས་པའི་བར་ལ། གལ་ཏེ་གཞན་དག་གིས་ཕྱིར་མི་ལྡོག་པ་ལ་སྤྱོད་པ་དང་ནི་དབང་པོ་དང༌། རྟགས་ཇི་ལྟ་བུ་འོང་པ་ལགས་ཞེས་ཡོངས་སུ་དྲིས་པ་ལ། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་དེ་རང་གི་མྱོང་བ་དང་སྟོང་པའི་སྟོང་པ་དང་མཚན་མ་མེད་པའི་ཆོས་ཀྱང་ཡོངས་སུ་མི་སྟོན་པ་ལ་ཕྱིར་ལྡོག་པའི་རྟགས་ཀྱི་ཆོས་དྲིས་ཀྱང་མི་འཆད་པ་དེ་ནི་སྔར་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱིས་ལུང་མ་བསྟན་པ་ཡིན་པར་རིག་པར་བྱའོ། །དེ་ཡན་ཆད་ཀྱིས་རྣམ་ཀུན་མངོན་རྫོགས་བཤད་ཟིན་ཏོ།།
[2-190] translation already produced for this document:
Thus it is said: From "if the practice" up to "should be known," it means that if others ask, "What are the practices, faculties, and signs of one who is irreversible?" and that bodhisattva does not reveal their own experience, nor the dharmas of emptiness and signlessness, and even when asked about the dharmas of the signs of irreversibility, does not explain them, it should be known that this is what the Buddha previously did not predict. With this, the complete explanation of the aspects of full awakening is finished.

[2-191] source:
སྐབས་ལྔ་པའི་རྩེ་མོ་མངོན་པར་རྟོགས་པའི་ངོ་བོ་ནི་ཆོས་སྐུའི་རྒྱུ་ལམ་རྣམ་གསུམ་མི་དམིགས་པ་གང་ཞིག་འབད་རྩོལ་མེད་པར་རྟོགས་པ་ལྷུན་གྲུབ་ཀྱི་བློ་ཐོབ་པའོ། །དེ་ཡང༌།དེ་ཡི་རྟགས་དང་རྣམ་འཕེལ་དང༌། །བརྟན་དང་སེམས་ཀུན་གནས་པ་དང༌། །མཐོང་ཞེས་བྱ་དང་བསྒོམ་པ་ཞེས། །བྱ་བའི་ལམ་ནི་སོ་སོ་ལ། །རྣམ་པར་རྟོག་པ་རྣམ་བཞི་ཡི། །གཉེན་པོ་རྣམ་པ་བཞི་དག་དང༌། །བར་ཆད་མེད་པའི་ཏིང་ངེ་འཛིན། །ལོག་པར་བསྒྲུབ་དང་བཅས་པ་ནི། །ཡང་དག་བྱང་ཆུབ་འབྲས་འབྱུང་བའི། །རྩེ་མོའི་མངོན་རྟོགས་ཡིན་པར་གསུངས། །ཞེས་པས། འདི་ལ་ཡོན་ཏན་རྒྱུད་ལ་བསྐྱེད་པའི་ཆ་ནས་དབྱེ་བ་བརྒྱད་ཀྱིས་བསྟན་ཏོ། །
[2-191] translation already produced for this document:
The essence of the peak clear realization of the fifth chapter is the attainment of a spontaneously present intellect that realizes, without effort, the non-apprehension of the three paths that are the causes of the dharmakāya. Regarding this, it is said:

"Its signs and the increase of aspects,
Stability and the abiding of the entire mind,
What is called 'seeing' and 'meditation,'
The paths of activity are distinct;
The four antidotes to the four types
Of conceptualization, along with
The uninterrupted meditative concentration
And the erroneous practice,
Are the peak clear realization
From which the fruit of true awakening arises."

Thus, it is taught through eight divisions from the perspective of generating these qualities within the continuum.

heading: **ལུང་བསྟན་ཐོབ་པ།**
translation: Thus it is said: Furthermore, in some human worlds, for people or sentient beings afflicted by many epidemic diseases caused by gods, nāgas, or the spirits of malevolent forces, if that bodhisattva, possessing benefit and compassion, recites a blessing of truth and thereby pacifies them, yet remains without any arrogant thought that "I am the one who possesses the power of blessing" and is a person in whom no pride arises, it should be known that this bodhisattva has been prophesied as irreversible.

[2-192] translation already produced for this document:
Thus it is said: From "Arhat" up to "should be known," it means that one does not desire, even in a dream, the level of an Arhat of the Lesser Vehicle, the wisdom of a Pratyekabuddha, or the splendor of the three realms; and if one sees in a dream that one sees the Buddhas, that they are seated on thrones, and that they are teaching the Dharma to sentient beings, it should be known that this is one who has been prophesied as irreversible from before.

[2-193] source:
ཞེས་གསུངས་ཏེ། ཡང་རྨི་ལམ་ནའམ་སད་པ་ན་གྲོང་ཁྱེར་ཚིག་པ་མཐོང་བ་ན་ཆོས་ཉིད་ཀྱི་བདེན་པའི་བྱིན་གྱིས་བརླབས་ཀྱིས་མེའི་ཕུང་པོ་འདི་དག་ཞི་བར་གྱུར་ཅིག་ཅེས་བརྗོད་པས་ཞི་བར་གྱུར་ན། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་དེ་ནི་ཕྱིར་མི་ལྡོག་པར་ལུང་བསྟན་པ་ཡིན་པར་རིག་པར་བྱའོ། །

Thus it is said: Furthermore, if, in a dream or while awake, one sees a burning city and, by saying, "By the blessing of the truth of the nature of phenomena, may these masses of fire be pacified," they are pacified, then it should be known that this bodhisattva has been prophesied as irreversible.

heading: **ལུང་མ་བསྟན་པ་ལས་བྱུང་བའི་བདུད་ཀྱི་ལས།**
translation: Thus it is said: If, when a bodhisattva sees sentient beings in the human world who are suffering from various illnesses caused by gods, nāgas, or spirits, they recite a blessing of truth out of a heart of benefit and compassion, and those illnesses are thereby pacified, yet they remain free from the arrogance of thinking, "I am the one who possesses the power of blessing," and are individuals in whom no pride arises, it should be known that this bodhisattva has been prophesied as irreversible.

heading: **བྱིན་བརླབས་ཀྱི་གཞི།**
translation: From the passage beginning with "If, however, that..." up to "...should be known," it is said: If a bodhisattva develops conceit, thinking that because they have attained and accomplished various blessings of truth—which are specific activities of Māra—they have been prophesied by the Buddha, or if a bodhisattva becomes conceited because another person has prophesied that they will become a Buddha, it should be known that such a person who harbors conceit is of little intelligence and lacks wisdom.

heading: **མིང་གི་གཞི།**
translation: Thus it is said: From the passage beginning with "From the basis of the name..." up to "...this is the name," it is said: The manner in which Māra gives a prophecy is that, because he looks for an opening based on the basis of the name, Māra approaches that bodhisattva and speaks thus: "In this way, here are the names of your father and mother, and the names of your lineage back through the generations; and when, at whatever time, you become a Buddha, this is the name, such as 'Moonlight,' that you will have." The person who develops conceit thinking this is of little intelligence.

heading: **སྦྱངས་པའི་ཡོན་ཏན་གྱི་གཞི།**
source: ཞེས་གསུངས་ཏེ། སྦྱངས་སྟོབས་རྣལ་འབྱོར་ཞེས་པ་ནས། རིག་པར་བྱ་ཞེས་པའི་བར་ལ། ཡང་སྦྱངས་པའི་ཡོན་ཏན་བཅུ་གཉིས་ཀྱི་སྡོམ་པ་སྟེ། དགོན་པ་དང༌། བསོད་སྙོམས་པ་དང༌། ཟས་ཕྱིས་མི་ལེན་པ་དང༌། སྟན་ཅིག་པ་དང༌། གཞི་ཇི་བཞིན་པ་དང༌། ཆོས་གོས་གསུམ་པ། དུར་ཁྲོད་པ། ཤིང་དྲུང་བ། ཙོག་པུ་བ། འདོད་པ་ཉུང་ཞིང་ཆོག་ཤེས་པ། རབ་ཏུ་དབེན་པ། རྐང་པ་སྐུད་པ་དང་བྲལ་བར་འཇམ་པོར་སྨྲ་ཞིང་ཚིག་ཉུང་བ་དང་ལྡན་ཞིང་བསྒོམ་པའི་རྣལ་འབྱོར་དང་ལྡན་པ་དང་བལྟ་བ་ཅི་འདྲ་བ་འབྱུང་བར་འགྱུར་བ་དེ་ལ། ཁྱོད་ནི་ད་ལྟར་མ་ཟད་ཀྱི་སྔོན་ཡང་ཡོན་ཏན་བཅུ་གཉིས་ཀྱི་ཚུལ་ཡང་ད་ལྟར་འདི་དང་འདྲའོ། །ཞེས་བརྗོད་དེ། བརྗོད་པ་དེས་སྐད་ཐོས་ནས་གང་ཐོབ་པ་ལ་ཡིད་ཆེས་ནས་ཁེངས་ཞིང་རློམ་སེམས་བྱེད་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ནི། བདུད་ཀྱི་སེམས་ཡོངས་སུ་བླང་ཞིང་གང་ཟག་བློ་ཆུང་བར་རིག་པར་བྱའོ། །
translation: Thus it is said: From the passage beginning with "The yoga of the power of training..." up to "...should be known," it is said: Furthermore, regarding the twelve ascetic practices—forest dwelling, alms collecting, not accepting food after time, eating in a single sitting, eating whatever is provided, wearing the three robes, dwelling in a charnel ground, dwelling at the root of a tree, dwelling in the open air, dwelling in a felt tent, being content with few desires, and being completely secluded—along with being gentle in speech, free from the entanglement of worldly concerns, having few words, possessing the yoga of meditation, and the nature of one's views: if one says to a bodhisattva, "Not only now, but in the past as well, your practice of the twelve ascetic qualities was just like this," and upon hearing such words, the bodhisattva becomes confident in what has been attained, becomes arrogant, and develops conceit, it should be known that such a bodhisattva has adopted the mind of Māra and is a person of little intelligence.

heading: **བཤད་པ།**
translation: It is said: From the passage beginning with "Constantly in villages..." up to "...is taught as seclusion," it is said: What is the seclusion of the Great Vehicle? It is that, apart from dwelling constantly in villages, large regions, and large towns, and striving to practice the six perfections for the sake of maturing sentient beings and accomplishing one's own enlightenment, one does not generate other desires—such as those of an Arhat, a Pratyekabuddha, or those attached to sensory objects. This is what is taught as the seclusion of the sons of the Sugatas, the Great Vehicle.

heading: **བཤད་པ།**
translation: It is said: Furthermore, any person of little intelligence who, due to the distinction of physical seclusion, dwells for many millions of years in mountain clefts five hundred leagues away from villages, in places filled with scorpions, snakes, birds, and wild beasts, yet does not know that this is not seclusion—because their mind is not secluded from the realization of existence and quiescence—is a bodhisattva of little intelligence who, having attained superior conceit through mere physical seclusion, dwells in such a state of what should be abandoned. And as for the bodhisattva who strives to benefit beings and has attained the concentration of the four meditative absorptions, the five powers, the five faculties, and the three gateways to liberation, the person of little intelligence who thinks, "This bodhisattva is practicing in a secluded wilderness," and thereby disparages them, is within the domain of Māra, the Victorious One has said.

This is what is taught as the seclusion of the sons of the Sugatas, the Great Vehicle.

heading: **བསྡུ་བ།**

A bodhisattva who, without knowing the measure of another bodhisattva’s spiritual warmth, becomes heated by afflictions, will themselves decline.

It is said: Furthermore, any person of little intelligence who, due to the distinction of physical seclusion, dwells for many millions of years in mountain clefts five hundred leagues away from villages, in places filled with scorpions, snakes, birds, and wild beasts, yet does not know that this is not seclusion—because their mind is not secluded from the realization of existence and quiescence—is a bodhisattva of little intelligence who, having attained superior conceit through mere physical seclusion, dwells in such a state of what should be abandoned. And as for the bodhisattva who strives to benefit beings and has attained the concentration of the four meditative absorptions, the five powers, the five faculties, and the three gateways to liberation, the person of little intelligence who thinks, "This bodhisattva is practicing in a secluded wilderness," and thereby disparages them, is within the domain of Māra, the Victorious One has said.

heading: **བསྟེན་པའི་ཚུལ།**
translation: From the passage "Therefore..." up to "...should be relied upon," it means that by means of such seclusion, one who seeks supreme enlightenment, possessing intense resolve and skillful means, must thoroughly subdue the pride that acts as an obstacle to the arising of the dharma-lineage. Just as a multitude of the sick rely dearly upon a skilled physician in order to cure their own illnesses, if one asks how one is to accomplish this perfection of wisdom through the means of intention, thought, and application, one should rely upon a spiritual friend—a guru—constantly and with respect, without distraction.

heading: **བཤད་པ།**
translation: It is said: From the passage "The Victors of the past..." up to "...is said to be," it means that the path traversed by all the Victors—those who have passed away, those who have not yet come, and those who currently reside in the directions—is this very set of six perfections, and no other. Thus, the Victors have explained that these six perfections are the supreme guide, because they bestow the fruit upon those who reside in the supreme awakening of the Great Vehicle, because they are the clarity that shows the path, because they are the lamp that illuminates through realization, and because they are the light that protects one from the sickness of the path.

heading: **དེ་ལས་ཀུན་ཉོན་མོངས་པ།**
translation: It is said: From the passage "Sentient beings..." up to "...the afflictions are taught," if one asks, "If all phenomena are empty, how can there be the two categories of the afflicted cycle of existence and the purified state of nirvāṇa?" it is because sentient beings, through their complete misunderstanding of grasping at a self, desire the food of sensory objects. Possessing a mind attached to the self and what belongs to the self—which are the causes of the cycle of existence—they are incited by the afflictions of that self and, accumulating karma from them, they cycle perpetually. However, the self and the phenomena of "what belongs to the self" to which they are attached do not exist in reality and are empty. Ordinary childish beings grasp at what is non-existent as if it were existent, which is like trying to tie a knot in empty space. Similarly, for example, when someone takes poison due to a mistaken perception, even though that poison has not actually entered into their physical substance, they will still be overcome by it. In the same way, ordinary childish beings who claim there is a self and what belongs to the self, because they perceive them as such, are born and die due to the power of grasping at them, despite their being truly non-existent. In short, it is taught that the extent to which there is grasping at a self and what belongs to the self is the extent to which there is the afflicted cycle of existence.
