In short, it is taught that the extent to which there is grasping at a self and what belongs to the self is the extent to which there is the afflicted cycle of existence.

heading: **ཚོགས་རྒྱ་ཆེན་པོ་བདེ་བླག་ཏུ་སོག་པ།**
translation: From the passage "In the Jambudvīpa..." up to "...should engage," the great benefit of meditating in that way is shown by means of an analogy. For example, if one were to take all the sentient beings in the Jambudvīpa without exception and, as a preliminary, generate the supreme intention of the bodhicitta to establish them in the supreme support, and then, as the main practice, engage in the application for a long time—for many tens of millions of thousands of years—by giving them abundant and excellent gifts to ripen them in the Buddha and in sentient beings, and finally, dedicate all that merit toward the cause of perfect awakening for the sake of the benefit of wandering beings; yet, if some person were to exert themselves in practicing the perfection of wisdom themselves and teaching it to others as previously explained, even if they were to do so in accordance with it for only a single day, the previously explained heap of merit would not approach even a hundredth part of that. Therefore, because of the cause, one should engage with diligence, practicing the perfection of wisdom constantly without being distracted by laziness or other activities.

translation: It is said: From the passage "a person previously..." up to "...as it changes," the words that demonstrate the perfection of wisdom must be accomplished easily and quickly. Just as in the analogy of finding a jewel, those who have entered the supreme path of enlightenment, having found the jewel-like perfection of wisdom, should not abandon it, for any yogin who possesses diligence will practice it. This is just like one who, having found and taken up the jewel mentioned before, wraps it carefully, hides it, and quickly proceeds to their own home, whereby the suffering of the world is pacified.

heading: **བསྒྲུབ་པ་གཞན་ཟིལ་གྱིས་གནོན་པ།**
translation: It is said: From the passage "like the sun free from clouds..." up to "...outshines," furthermore, for example, when the sun, which possesses a network of rays and is free from clouds, rises, it destroys all the darkness of the dense, black gloom of the opposing side and causes light to appear. By that, the light of all the fireflies and living spirits of the favorable side, as well as the light of the hosts of stars and the light of the moon, are all outshone by the light of the sun. Just so, a bodhisattva who practices the supreme perfection of wisdom, which is like the sun, practices emptiness and the signless; and through skillful means, having destroyed the dense gloom of ignorance that views the opposing side as a self and as phenomena, they outshine with the non-conceptual the many conceptual virtues of the favorable side—the virtues of the śrāvakas that are conducive to merit and conducive to liberation, the virtues of the pratyekabuddhas, and the virtues of the bodhisattvas of the Great Vehicle.

heading: **ལྷ་མིའི་མགོན་དུ་གྱུར་པ།**
translation: It is said: From the passage "like a prince..." up to "...what need is there to mention," the fact that one who practices the supreme path becomes a glory to gods and humans is like the analogy of the young prince. In that same way, a bodhisattva who practices the perfection of wisdom and possesses skillful means also heals the illness of the afflictions; they bestow a gift like nectar, and by the power of that, gods and humans, being joyful, come into their presence. One generates the hope that, since this bodhisattva, even now in the time of being a son of the Victor, strives to benefit many sentient beings, what need is there to mention the benefit they will provide to sentient beings when they eventually dwell in the state of having awakened as a King of Dharma?

It is said: From the passage "like the sun free from clouds..." up to "...outshines," furthermore, for example, when the sun, which possesses a network of rays and is free from clouds, rises, it destroys all the darkness of the dense, black gloom of the opposing side and causes light to appear. By that, the light of all the fireflies and living spirits of the favorable side, as well as the light of the hosts of stars and the light of the moon, are all outshone by the light of the sun. Just so, a bodhisattva who practices the supreme perfection of wisdom, which is like the sun, practices emptiness and the signless; and through skillful means, having destroyed the dense gloom of ignorance that views the opposing side as a self and as phenomena, they outshine with the non-conceptual the many conceptual virtues of the favorable side—the virtues of the śrāvakas that are conducive to merit and conducive to liberation, the virtues of the pratyekabuddhas, and the virtues of the bodhisattvas of the Great Vehicle.

It is said: From the passage "like a prince..." up to "...what need is there to mention," the fact that one who practices the supreme path becomes a glory to gods and humans is like the analogy of the young prince. In that same way, a bodhisattva who practices the perfection of wisdom and possesses skillful means also heals the illness of the afflictions; they bestow a gift like nectar, and by the power of that, gods and humans, being joyful, come into their presence. One generates the hope that, since this bodhisattva, even now in the time of being a son of the Victor, strives to benefit many sentient beings, what need is there to mention the benefit they will provide to sentient beings when they eventually dwell in the state of having awakened as a King of Dharma?

heading: **ལྷ་མིའི་མགོན་དུ་གྱུར་པ།**
translation: It is said: From the passage "whenever the wise" up to "how could they find an opening," it means that whenever those wise bodhisattvas are endowed with intense aspiration, love, and compassion, and their practice is to contemplate the meaning of the supreme perfection of wisdom without regard for day or night, at that time, the body, mind, and speech of that bodhisattva are like a bird moving through the sky, free from the two extremes and without harm. As for Māra and his black-hearted retinue who belong to his circle, even if they look for an opening, how could they find one? They find no opening at all.

heading: **ཞོར་ལ་ཚོགས་པ།**
translation: It is said: From the passage "whenever a bodhisattva" up to "learning in this teaching of the Buddha," it means that at whatever time some bodhisattvas engage in physical conflict, verbal dispute, and harbor mutually discordant and angry minds toward one another, at that time, Māra and his retinue become joyful, their bodies feel supremely at ease, and they think: "These two bodhisattvas who are fighting and disputing are becoming far removed from the wisdom of the Victors, so my own purpose will be accomplished," and they become mentally delighted. Regarding the actual situation, those two bodhisattvas become distant from wisdom and their causes become fierce and predatory; thus, both of them fall away from the vow of the mind-generation they had previously made. If one asks how they fall away: since that intention is hateful and devoid of patience, how could there be awakening? There is none. At such a time, Māra and his faction become extremely joyful. In particular, if any bodhisattva who has not yet received a prophecy begins to feel angry and starts a dispute with a bodhisattva who has previously received a prophecy, because they are possessed of the fault of the ash of defilement, they must don the armor of patience for as many eons as the number of such moments of thought. The antidote to that negativity, or the method to reverse it, is patience; for all the Buddhas have also attained the supreme awakening by cultivating the perfection of patience. Therefore, thinking "this hateful mind is not good," one should generate the mindfulness of regret, confess individually through various antidotes, restrain such thoughts and actions in the future, and not take pleasure in what was previously done; this is what is meant by learning in this teaching of the Buddha.

heading: **དགེ་བ་ཐམས་ཅད་བསྡུད་པ།**
source: ཞེས་གསུངས་ཏེ། དེ་ལ་སྤྱིར་དབང་པོ་ཉི་ཤུ་རྩ་གཉིས་ལས། རྣམ་བྱང་གི་དབང་པོ་ནི། དད་པའི་དབང་པོ་དང༌། དྲན་པའི་དང༌། བརྩོན་འགྲུས་ཀྱི་དང༌། ཏིང་ངེ་འཛིན་གྱི་དང༌། ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་དང༌། མི་ཤེས་པ་ཀུན་ཤེས་པ་ཡི་དང༌། ཀུན་ཤེས་པ་དང༌། ཀུན་ཤེས་པ་གྲོལ་བས་དང་བརྒྱད། ཉོན་མོངས་པ་འཁོར་བའི་དང༌། མིག་གི་དབང་པོ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ལྔ་དང༌། ཡིད་ཀྱི་དང་ཡིད་བདེ་མི་བདེ་གཉིས་དང༌། ཚོར་བའི་བདེ་སྡུག་བཏང་སྙོམས་གསུམ་དང༌། སྲོག་གི་དབང་པོ་དང༌། ཕོ་མོའི་དབང་པོ་གཉིས་ཏེ་བཅུ་བཞི་དེ་ལྟར་ན་དབང་པོ་ཉི་ཤུ་རྩ་གཉིས་ཡོད་པ་ལས། དཔེར་ན་སྲོག་གི་དབང་པོ་གཅིག་པུ་འགགས་ན་དབང་པོ་རྩ་ཅིག་པོ་གཞན། གང་དག་ཇི་སྙེད་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་འགགས་པར་འགྱུར་བས་སྲོག་གི་དབང་པོར་དབང་པོ་གཞན་རྣམས་འདུས་པའོ། །དཔེ་དེ་ལྟར་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལ་སྤྱོད་པའི་མཁས་པ་མཆོག་ཏུ་གྱུར་པ་རྣམས་ཀྱིས། ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལྔ་ཐམས་ཅད་མི་དམིགས་པར་ཤེས་པའི་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་འདིར་ནི་འདུས་པར་གསུངས་སོ། །
translation: Thus it is said. Regarding that, in general, among the twenty-two faculties, the faculties of the path of purification are eight: the faculty of faith, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of diligence, the faculty of concentration, the faculty of wisdom, the faculty of "knowing the unknown," the faculty of "knowing all," and the faculty of "having known all." The faculties of the defiled cycle of existence are fourteen: the five faculties such as the eye faculty, the two of mind and mental happiness and unhappiness, the three of physical pleasure, suffering, and equanimity, the life faculty, and the two faculties of male and female. Thus, there are twenty-two faculties. Just as when the life faculty alone ceases, all the other twenty-one faculties cease, and therefore the other faculties are included within the life faculty; in that same way, it is said that for those supreme experts who practice the perfection of wisdom, all five perfections are included within this perfection of wisdom, which is the wisdom that knows them to be non-apprehended.

heading: **དགེ་བ་ཐམས་ཅད་བསྡུད་པ།**
translation: Thus it is said. From the phrase "the skillful bodhisattva" up to the phrase "therefore they train," it means that whatever qualities of the śrāvakas exist, and likewise all the qualities of the pratyekabuddhas, the skillful bodhisattva trains in them for the sake of others; and those bodhisattvas do not abide in those qualities by way of attachment, nor do they generate desire for them by way of savoring their taste. Thinking that these qualities of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are things to be trained in by bodhisattvas for the sake of others, they therefore train others in them as well.

Thus it is said. Regarding that, in general, among the twenty-two faculties, the faculties of the path of purification are eight: the faculty of faith, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of diligence, the faculty of concentration, the faculty of wisdom, the faculty of "knowing the unknown," the faculty of "knowing all," and the faculty of "having known all." Just as when the life faculty alone ceases, all the other twenty-one faculties cease, and therefore the other faculties are included within the life faculty; in that same way, it is said that for those supreme experts who practice the perfection of wisdom, all five perfections are included within this perfection of wisdom, which is the wisdom that knows them to be non-apprehended.

heading: **མི་རྟོག་པའི་སྤྱོད་པ་ཐོབ་པ།**
translation: From the phrase "up to" to the phrase "practices the pacification," it means that any bodhisattva who fully understands that all phenomena, such as form and so forth, are emptiness—being empty by nature—as well as the signless—being empty of causes—and the wishless—being empty of results—is a practitioner who does not seek awakening through the two types of grasping and fixation, nor through the two types of selflessness; such a one is diligent in the supreme perfection of wisdom that knows without apprehending. For example, the sky in the east and the sky in the west do not have differences in height or depth, nor in length or breadth, nor are there such contradictions, and no person can attain the meaning of their being distinct. In the same way, the three doors of a bodhisattva who is skilled in practicing the perfection of wisdom that knows without apprehending are not like the sky, which is an analogy for having no conceptualization at all; rather, the bodhisattva practices the pacification of these conceptualizations of nearness and distance.

heading: **བདུད་ཀྱིས་མི་རྫི་བ།**
translation: Thus it is said. From the phrase "equal to the sands of the Ganges" to the phrase "possessing blessings," even if all the sentient beings in fields as numerous as the sands of the Ganges were to adopt the intention of examining everything and become Māras, and even if each of them were to manifest as many emanations as there are individual hairs on their bodies, all those Māras would still be unable to create an obstacle for that wise bodhisattva. heading: **བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ངོས་བཟུང་བ།**
translation: From the phrase "the dharmadhātu is suchness" to the phrase "is not a dwelling," one does not dwell on the basis, the dharmadhātu of phenomena, by way of mental attachment; rather, one dwells without dwelling on any object of apprehension, just as clouds appear in the sky without dwelling there. From the phrase "this training" to the phrase "train in this perfection," [it is explained that] this non-abiding training is what the Guide has fully declared to be the training of the path of the Great Vehicle. Among all the trainings that have been mentioned, such as the higher training in ethical discipline and the higher training in mind, this training in wisdom is the most supreme and unsurpassed. Therefore, any wise person who wishes to reach the perfection of all trainings should train in this perfection of wisdom, which is the uncommon path of the Buddhas.

heading: **ཕྱི་རྟེན་འབྲེལ།**
translation: From the phrase "tree and fruit" to the phrase "no increase," [it is explained that] just as with external dependent origination, all the happiness of sentient beings and all the phenomena that are produced arise through the practice of the supreme perfection of wisdom, which follows along with them; yet, for the perfection of wisdom that arises, there is never any exhaustion into a lesser state, nor is there any increase into a greater state.

source: ཞེས་གསུངས་ཏེ། སེམས་ཅན་ཐ་མ་འབྲིང་དང་ཞེས་པ་ནས། ཐོབ་པར་འགྱུར་ཞེས་པའི་བར་ལ། ཡང་ན་རྟེན་ཅིང་འབྲེལ་བར་འབྱུང་བ་སེམས་ཅན་ཐ་མ་ངན་འགྲོ་གསུམ། འབྲིང་མི་དང༌། མཆོག་ཏུ་གྱུར་པའི་རིགས་ཇི་སྙེད་ཡོད་པ་དེ་དག་ཀུན་ཏུ་རྒྱུ་འབྲས་དང༌། དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་མི་ཤེས་པའི་རྒྱུ་མ་རིག་པ་ལས་འབྱུང་བར་བདེ་བར་གཤེགས་པས་གསུངས་སོ། །དེ་ལས་དང་ཉོན་མོངས་པའི་རྐྱེན་རྣམས་འཚོགས་ནས་ཁམས་གསུམ་གྱི་སྡུག་བསྔལ་གྱི་འཁྲུལ་འཁོར་རབ་ཏུ་འབྱུང་ལ། རྒྱུ་མ་རིག་པའི་འཁྲུལ་འཁོར་དེ་ནི་ཟད་པའང་མེད་ལ་འཕེལ་བ་ཡང་མེད་དོ། །དཔེ་དེ་བཞིན་དུ་མཐར་ཕྱིན་པའི་ཡེ་ཤེས་ཚུལ་ཅེས་པས་བསྒོམ་པའི་ལམ་དང༌། སྒོ་ཅེས་པས་མཐོང་བའི་ལམ་དང༌། ཐབས་ཅེས་པས་སྦྱོར་བའི་ལམ་དང༌། རྩ་བ་ཅེས་པས་ཚོགས་ལམ་སོགས་ཇི་སྙེད་པ་ཀུན་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པའི་མཆོག་འདི་ལས་འབྱུང་ངོ༌། །མ་རིག་པའི་བག་ཆགས་ཀྱི་ས་དང་ཟག་པ་མེད་པའི་ལས་ཀྱི་རྐྱེན་རྣམས་འཚོགས་ནས་བསམ་གྱིས་མི་ཁྱབ་པའི་འཆི་འཕོ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ལས་ཀྱི་འཁྲུལ་འཁོར་རབ་ཏུ་བྱུང་ལ། ཆོས་ཀྱི་དབྱིངས་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལ་ཟད་པ་མེད་ཅིང་འཕེལ་བའང་མེད་དོ། །བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གང་ལ་ལ་ཞིག་ངོ་བོ་རྟེན་ཅིང་འབྲེལ་བར་འབྱུང་བ་ལ། རང་བཞིན་སྐྱེ་བ་མེད་པ་དང་ཟད་ཅིང་འགག་པ་མེད་པར་ཤེས་པའི་ཤེས་རབ་འདི་ཤེས་ཏེ། དཔེར་ན་ཉི་མ་སྤྲིན་མེད་པའི་འོད་ཟེར་འཕྲོ་བས། མུན་པའི་ཚོགས་བསལ་བ་ལྟར། ཐོག་མ་མེད་པའི་དུས་ཀྱི་མ་རིག་པ་གཉིས་ཀྱི་འཐིབས་པོ་བཅོམ་ནས་མཐོང་ལམ་དང་བསྒོམ་ལམ་གྱི་རང་འབྱུང་གི་ཡེ་ཤེས་ཐོབ་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །དེ་ཡན་ཆད་ཀྱིས་གཙོ་བོ་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་རྒྱས་པར་བསྟན་ཏོ། །
translation: Thus it is said. From the phrase "sentient beings, lowest, middling, and" to the phrase "will be attained," [it is explained that] the Sugata has taught that dependent origination—all the various types of sentient beings, whether lowest (the three lower realms), middling (humans), or supreme (the noble lineages)—arises from ignorance, which is the cause of not knowing the causal results and suchness. From that, the conditions of karma and afflictions gather, and the wheel of suffering of the three realms arises; yet, that wheel of ignorance, which is the cause, has no exhaustion and no increase. In the same way, the phrase "the manner of perfected wisdom" refers to the path of meditation, "gate" refers to the path of seeing, "method" refers to the path of preparation, and "root" refers to the path of accumulation and so forth; all of these arise from this supreme perfection of wisdom. When the ground of the latent tendencies of ignorance and the conditions of undefiled karma gather, the inconceivable wheel of karma, such as death and transmigration, arises; yet, for the dharmadhātu, the perfection of wisdom, there is no exhaustion and no increase. Any bodhisattva who knows this wisdom—which understands that the essence of dependent origination is by nature unborn and without exhaustion or cessation—is like the sun in a cloudless sky radiating its light to dispel the masses of darkness; by destroying the density of the two types of ignorance from beginningless time, they will attain the self-arisen primordial wisdom of the path of seeing and the path of meditation. With this, the primary perfection of wisdom has been explained in detail.

heading: འབྲས་བུ་དམ་པའི་རྟེན་བྱེད་པ།
translation: Regarding the passage from "possessing great power" to "not training for the sake of exhaustion": A bodhisattva who possesses the power of the perfection of wisdom and possesses great power dwells for the sake of others even while possessing meditative concentration and the like, the four [factors]. There are many who rely upon these by grasping at them as signs and tasting their flavor, yet there is no one who dwells in them continuously. Even though they do not dwell in them, they engage with them. However, in these four—which include the six or eighteen limbs of the four meditative concentrations—the bodhisattva of the Great Vehicle finds the basis for attaining the path of seeing and the supreme or ultimate perfect buddhahood. Having attained the supreme perfection of wisdom that possesses all of these, they dwell in the stainless meditative concentration, and they also experience the four supreme meditative stabilizations of the four formless spheres for a short time for the sake of others. For what purpose is this? These meditative concentrations and meditative stabilizations are for the sake of supreme enlightenment; they are not for the sake of the bodhisattva training to exhaust their own defilements as in the case of the śrāvakas.

heading: **མ་ཆགས་པའི་ཁྱད་པར།**
translation: Regarding the passage from "this is the collection of qualities" to "does not dwell in phenomena": What is this marvelous bodhisattva who possesses the collection of qualities? It is a bodhisattva who, having dwelt in the four meditative concentrations and the four formless meditative stabilizations, does not savor them by way of grasping at signs. Those who dwell in them, having made a prayer for the desire realm, if this body were to disintegrate, even though they are free from the desire for the desire realm, they are born again in the desire realm just as they were before, in accordance with the intention of their prayer. For example, it is like a person such as the universal monarch Yaśas-ananta who, having never previously gone to the supreme divine city in the divine realm, goes there later; having seen and enjoyed those realms that are fully occupied by the gods, if he were to return to this Jambudvīpa with a malicious mind, he would not yearn for the divine realm. Similarly, a yogi who is diligent, holding the supreme qualities through the meditative stabilization of non-apprehension, dwells in the four meditative concentrations and the four meditative stabilizations, and then dwells again in the desire realm without having any attachment to the flavor of the previous meditative concentrations. Just as a lotus in water is not soiled by the water, even though they are born in the desire realm, the child-like being does not dwell in the phenomena of desire.

translation: Thus it is said. From "if a bodhisattva" up to "should be known as such," if a bodhisattva who has attained and abides in the previously explained meditative concentration and dhyāna gives rise to the intention of desiring to attain the vehicle of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, then even though they are in meditative equipoise and their mind abides in dhyāna, they are distracted by thoughts of the discordant factors of the Great Vehicle and the like, and because they decline from attaining the qualities of a buddha, such as the powers, it is like a ship breaking upon a dangerous ocean. On the other hand, even if a bodhisattva engages in and strives toward form, sound, and likewise smell, taste, touch, and the five objects of desire without attachment, they are separated from the discordant factors of the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha vehicles, and if their mind rejoices in attaining the supreme, perfect awakening, then because their mind does not waver from what is to be attained, it should be known that the heroic bodhisattva is always in meditative equipoise. Having thus far explained the stage of the "peak," the essence of the sixth stage, the "gradual practice," which is not instantaneous and in which post-meditative attainment is primary, is the meditation on the three—the basis, the path, and the result—of the dharmakāya as non-referential, while simultaneously putting into practice the gradual conduct of awakening. Furthermore, since the non-attached activity within the appearance of post-meditative attainment is a virtuous practice, this text explains it from the perfection of vigor down to the perfection of generosity. Jñānapāda holds that it is explained through the six benefits of the situation. There are thirteen divisions here, and this text is complete in its meaning without any gaps.

[2-264] translation already produced for this document:
From "great being" up to "does not seek," the great being acts solely to bring the sentient beings to be trained to full maturity, to purify the buddhafields, and to complete the accumulation of their own six perfections; it is not for the sake of attachment to desired pleasures. If one asks, "Does one who abides in that meditative concentration take birth in the formless realm?" the answer is that one does not, for that would result in a decline in the practice of the bodhisattva’s qualities and perfections. Thus, one does not seek to take birth in the formless realm.

ཅེས་གསུངས་ཏེ། དཔེར་ན་མི་ཞིག་ཞེས་པ་ནས། འདོད་ཁམས་འཇུག་ཞེས་པའི་བར་ལ། རིན་པོ་ཆེའི་གཏེར་རྙེད་པའི་མིའི་དཔེ་དེ་བཞིན་དུ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་སྦྱངས་པ་དང་ལྡན་པ་མཁས་པ་གཞན་གྱི་དོན་བྱེད་པ་ལས་དགའ་བ་དང༌། གཞན་ལ་བདེ་བ་སྦྱིན་པ་ཡང་བསམ་གཏན་བཞི་དང་ཏིང་ངེ་འཛིན་བཞིའི་ཞི་བ་བཞི་ཐོབ་ནས། དེ་ལ་ཡང་མ་ཆགས་པར་བསམ་གཏན་གྱི་བདེ་བ་དང་ལྡན་པས་བསམ་གཏན་གྱི་ཏིང་ངེ་འཛིན་ཐོབ་པའི་ཕྱིར་བཏང་སྟེ། འགྲོ་བ་རྣམས་ལ་སྙིང་བརྩེ་བ་དང་ལྡན་པས་ཕྱིར་ཡང་འདོད་པའི་ཁམས་སུ་འཇུག་པར་འདོད་དོ། །
[2-265] translation already produced for this document:
Thus it is said. From "like a person" up to "enters the desire realm," just as in the analogy of the person who has found a treasure of precious jewels, the wise bodhisattva who possesses training finds joy in working for the benefit of others and in bestowing happiness upon them. Having attained the four dhyānas and the fourfold tranquility of the meditative concentrations, they do not become attached to them; rather, they relinquish the meditative concentration they have attained, even though they possess the bliss of dhyāna, and because they possess compassion for all beings, they wish to enter the desire realm once again.

heading: **གུས་པས་འགྲོ་བ།**
translation: From the passage beginning with "sentient beings and individuals" up to "burns that very thing," the pure example of the diligence of the ritual of other sentient beings and individuals is, conventionally, the practice of the perfection of diligence while exerting oneself without conceptualization. Just as in the example of the maidservant, for the sake of the great awakening that is to be attained, bodhisattvas who have entered into the supreme intention should also abide in thought and action as if they were servants to all sentient beings. By acting in this way, one attains awakening from this and the qualities of the stages will be perfected. If one does not act in this way, but instead acts with arrogance and hatred, one burns one's own continuum, just as when fire arises from grass and wood, it burns that very grass and wood.

heading: **རང་བདེ་བ་ལ་མ་ཆགས་པ།**
translation: Thus it is said. From the passage beginning with "having abandoned one's own happiness" up to "exerting oneself," it is again like this: having abandoned the happiness of one's own desire and form realms, one exerts oneself without day or night for the needs of other sentient beings, with a mind that does not hope for a return.

heading: **གཞན་གྱི་དོན་ལ་མི་སྐྱོ་བ།**
translation: Thus it is said. From the passage beginning with "for an only child" up to "abide," it means: just as a mother serves her only child with affection, in that same way, abide in working for the benefit of others with a sincere heart and without any mental weariness. By this, the occasion of the dharmakāya is taught.

[2-272] translation already produced for this document:
Thus it is said. From the passage beginning with "bodhisattva" up to "without negligence," it means: any bodhisattva who wishes to remain in the cycle of existence for a long time yet, and who is a practitioner diligent in the tasks of benefiting sentient beings, engaging in buddha-fields, and perfecting their own accumulations—if that practitioner does not give rise to even an atom's worth of a mind that is weary of the difficult practices or the long duration of time, then they are possessed of the perfection of diligence and are without negligence in the intention and application of the Great Vehicle.

[2-273] source:

heading: **སྦྱོར་བ་བྱ་དཀའ་བས་ཞུམ་པ།**
translation: Thus it is said. From the passage beginning with "If someone" up to "has become," it means: furthermore, if the Buddha speaks to some individual saying, "In order to attain full awakening, the example of the hardship to be practiced is that after performing the hardship of demolishing Mount Meru, one will attain that supreme, perfect awakening," and if that person generates a mind of weariness toward such asceticism and contemplates the scale of Mount Meru, at that time, that bodhisattva has become lazy and sluggish.

heading: **བཟློག་པ།**
translation: From the passage beginning with "fully ripening beings" up to "like the sky and the earth," it means: if some individual who grasps at entities thinks, "I shall perform the task of fully ripening beings," and strives with a body, speech, and mind that are grasped as a self, then because the perception of the true existence of a person as a self remains, they become lazy due to the power of that. The example of how such a person is far from attaining the omniscience of a Buddha is like the distance between the sky and the earth.

heading: **ངོ་བོ།**
translation: From the passage beginning with "If from another" up to "is wise," it means: if one hears harsh words of abuse from another person, such as being told one is being killed, the wise bodhisattva is joyful, thinking that on the conventional level, practicing patience is a source of happiness. However, on the ultimate level, if one examines by focusing on who is the speaker, who is the person hearing, what is the reason, what is the object being expressed, and for what purpose, then because one possesses the supreme perfection of patience that is certain regarding the phenomena that are the objects of such focus, one is wise.

heading: **འབྲས་བུ།**
translation: From the passage beginning with "Whatever bodhisattva" up to "is wise," it means: regarding the aforementioned bodhisattva who possesses such excellent qualities of the merit of patience, if someone were to fill this great trichiliocosm with the seven types of precious substances and offer them with faith and respect to the Buddhas who know the worlds, the śrāvaka arhats, and the pratyekabuddhas, the merit of the heap of generosity would not even be worth a hundredth or a hundred-millionth part of the merit of one who has practiced patience. Thus, the body of one who abides in patience becomes completely pure, possessing the marks and secondary signs, or the radiance and strength; the thirty-two marks, such as the wheels on the palms and soles, and boundless power and strength arise. Furthermore, because they proclaim to other sentient beings the supreme emptiness of all phenomena, they are wise, knowing that the beings who have faith and joy in one who possesses such patience are truly in accordance with reality.

heading: **ཕན་ཡོན།**
translation: Thus it is said. From the passage beginning with "Bodhisattva" up to "surpasses," it means: in this way, when a wise bodhisattva has practiced such patience, if he dedicates that virtue of generating a patient mind in the present moment toward the supreme enlightenment, then that hero, through the virtue of patience toward all worldly harms, will surpass all the virtues of the Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and however many realms of sentient beings there are, by means of the purity of that patience.

heading: **མདོར་བསྟན་པ།**
translation: From the passage beginning with "By ethical discipline" up to "dedicate to enlightenment," it means: through the ethical discipline of the Great Vehicle, those who have pacified suffering and agitation do not become [limited to] the paths of suffering or the stages of the śrāvakas; likewise, they do not become [limited to] the exalted ones. heading: **རྒྱས་པར་བཤད་པ།**
translation: Thus it is said. From the passage beginning with "If an arhat or pratyekabuddha" up to "abiding in the perfection," it means: if one desires to attain the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha or an arhat through that virtue, then one’s ethical discipline of the Great Vehicle is flawed, one’s practice is of little purpose, one is unwise, and likewise, one has fallen away from the conduct of enlightenment. Conversely, if one dedicates it completely without apprehending the supreme peace of enlightenment, then even if one remains in the state of a householder and strives to enjoy the objects of desire, one is abiding in the perfection of ethical discipline of the Great Vehicle.

heading: **རྒྱས་པར་བཤད་པ།**
translation: Thus it is said. From the passage beginning with "If a bodhisattva" up to "extremely heavy," it means: now, explaining the faults and virtues, if a bodhisattva who has become a householder engages in the five objects of desire, yet until the essence of enlightenment takes refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha of Noble Ones, and does not separate from keeping in mind the omniscient Buddha with the thought, "I shall accomplish the Buddhahood that is to be attained for the sake of sentient beings," then one should know that such a wise person, who has the continuity of training, abides in the perfection of ethical discipline of the definitive Great Vehicle, because there is no fault in the intention and practice of the Great Vehicle. Conversely, if one practices the ten paths of virtuous action for ten million eons, yet generates the desire to attain the state of a pratyekabuddha or an arhat as what is to be accomplished, then because the bodhicitta has degenerated, a fault has arisen in the Great Vehicle ethical discipline, and this is the fault of having degenerated in ethical discipline. Generating the mind that desires to attain the lesser fruit, such as that of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha, is even more extremely heavy than the occurrence of the four root downfalls of a monk, which include the mind of transgression.

From the passage beginning with "If a bodhisattva" up to "extremely heavy," it means: now, explaining the faults and virtues, if a bodhisattva who has become a householder engages in the five objects of desire, yet until the essence of enlightenment takes refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha of Noble Ones, and does not separate from keeping in mind the omniscient Buddha with the thought, "I shall accomplish the Buddhahood that is to be attained for the sake of sentient beings," then one should know that such a wise person, who has the continuity of training, abides in the perfection of ethical discipline of the definitive Great Vehicle, because there is no fault in the intention and practice of the Great Vehicle. Having completely abandoned the perception of the truth of wisdom and the perception of the truth of sentient beings, by proceeding on the path of the Great Vehicle, they are said to abide in the bodhisattva's perfection of ethical discipline.

heading: **ཕན་ཡོན།**
translation: Thus it is said. From the passage beginning with "If a bodhisattva" up to "spoken of by the Guide," the faults and qualities of that very subject are explained: if a bodhisattva, through a lack of skill in means, practices the path of the Victorious One, and—thinking, "These are possessed of ethical discipline, and these are transgressors of ethical discipline"—clings to the meaning of signs, then because of a view of self, they enter into a perception of truth regarding various distinct things. This is a great transgression of ethical discipline in the Great Vehicle, for their vow-based ethical discipline is impaired, and for one who holds to it in that way, that ethical discipline of the three spheres of purity is absent. Conversely, for a person who lacks the perception of permanence, the perception of a self, and the perception of the truth of sentient beings, and who is free from the desire of perceiving distinct truths, the cause for transgression is exhausted; so how could it be said that they lack the vow? It does not exist. Therefore, for anyone who knows all phenomena to be of an equal nature, there is no conceit of "vow" or "non-vow," and this lack of conceit is what the Guides—that is, the fully enlightened Buddhas—have called the bodhisattva's vow of ethical discipline. Up to this point, the meaning of the perfection of ethical discipline has been analyzed and explained.

[2-299] translation already produced for this document:
Thus it is said. From the passage beginning with "If a bodhisattva" up to "spoken of by the Guide," the faults and qualities of that very subject are explained: if a bodhisattva, through a lack of skill in means, practices the path of the Victorious One, and—thinking, "These are possessed of ethical discipline, and these are transgressors of ethical discipline"—clings to the meaning of signs, then because of a view of self, they enter into a perception of truth regarding various distinct things. This is a great transgression of ethical discipline in the Great Vehicle, for their vow-based ethical discipline is impaired, and for one who holds to it in that way, that ethical discipline of the three spheres of purity is absent. Conversely, for a person who lacks the perception of permanence, the perception of a self, and the perception of the truth of sentient beings, and who is free from the desire of perceiving distinct truths, the cause for transgression is exhausted; so how could it be said that they lack the vow? It does not exist. Therefore, for anyone who knows all phenomena to be of an equal nature, there is no conceit of "vow" or "non-vow," and this lack of conceit is what the Guides—that is, the fully enlightened Buddhas—have called the bodhisattva's vow of ethical discipline. Up to this point, the meaning of the perfection of ethical discipline has been analyzed and explained.

heading: **རྗེས་འགྲོ།**
translation: From "a pure mind" up to "there is no basis": furthermore, regarding any sentient being whose continuum is completely purified, they possess a morality that is free from such arrogance, and they give away objects of generosity without viewing pleasant or unpleasant things with attachment or aversion. They give away internal things such as their head and limbs, and they have no mind that shrinks from giving. They give away all external things and have no attachment to what has been given. Having understood that internal and external phenomena—the defilements of cyclic existence and the purified phenomena of nirvāṇa—are by nature selfless, unreal, illusory, and without essence, the bodhisattva has no mind that shrinks or is unable to give away even their own flesh. If that is absent, then it goes without saying that there is no shrinking from giving away external objects. If one realizes that the basis is selfless, then to be stingy about it is to have no basis.

heading: **སྙིང་རྗེས་ཟིན་པས་དགའ་བའི་གཏོང་བ།**
translation: From "at that time the bodhisattva" up to "it is not like that": at that time, knowing that sentient beings become hungry ghosts and poor because they have not practiced generosity, bodhisattvas, being seized by compassion, aspire to the intention of giving and always practice it with great generosity, without attachment. The reason for such liberality is that, having understood that all the enjoyments of the four continents, however well-adorned, are like a glob of spittle, they find joy in giving them away to others; it is not like that joy which arises from acquiring the continents after having given them to others.

heading: **དོན་རྒྱ་ཆེ་བར་གཏོང་བ།**
translation: It is said: From "having given a gift" up to "seeking the excellent," furthermore, having given a gift, one does not dwell upon or become attached to the material object; the manner in which that bodhisattva never has any expectation for the maturation of the result is that all who are skilled in giving in this way give without attachment to or expectation of cause and effect. Because the power of their intention is great, even a small cause given will result in excellent, vast, and immeasurable fruit. Since there are as many sentient beings as there are in the three realms of existence—above the earth, below the earth, and upon the earth—having grasped the limit of thorough investigation, even if one were to give excellent material gifts for an infinite eon to the fields of merit—the buddhas, arhats, and pratyekabuddhas—if one then seeks the result of a śrāvaka, that is of inferior intelligence.

heading: **གཞན་ཟིལ་གྱི་གནོན་པ།**
translation: It is said: From "bodhisattva" up to "outshine," furthermore, a skilled bodhisattva, even though not engaged in material objects, possesses merit through skill in means; by rejoicing in the objects of merit of those in cyclic existence and nirvana, and by dedicating that merit arising from rejoicing as a cause for supreme, excellent enlightenment for the sake of sentient beings, through this dedication, they outshine the virtue of all beings, from the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas downwards. For example, even if there were a great heap of inferior gems, a single precious vaiḍūrya gem would outshine that entire collection of gems. Similarly, the heaps of generosity of all beings, from the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas downwards—including their vast fields, times, and material objects—are outshone by the virtue of a bodhisattva that arises from subsequent rejoicing.

heading: སྦྱིན་པའི་བསོད་ནམས་བསྡུ་བ།
translation: From "If a bodhisattva" up to "like the waxing moon," the perfection of generosity without attachment is praised by way of an analogy: if a bodhisattva gives gifts to sentient beings, does not claim the merit of having given the gift as their own, and is without stinginess or reluctance regarding the objects to be given, then those roots of virtue arising from that non-attached generosity will increase in great power, just as the disk of the moon, possessing light and free from clouds, increases from the waxing phase onwards. Up to this point, the meaning of how to train in the six perfections of the Great Vehicle has been explained in detail and in sequence. This explains the result of training in that way; since the result of gradual cultivation arises in the continuum simultaneously, the essence of the seventh chapter—the practice of realizing full enlightenment in a single moment—is called the simultaneous cultivation of all pure phenomena, which is the ultimate, having shown the power of the intellect where the three—the basis, path, and cause of the dharmakāya—are not apprehended. As it is said: "Because the Sage, in order to perfectly gather all that is without defilement, even through each one such as generosity, realizes full enlightenment in a single moment." Therefore, here it is explained through six benefits, and according to Jñānapāda, the seventh chapter is explained by the single line "this teaching is now completed," and what follows is considered the eighth. This shows four divisions.

It is said: From "bodhisattva" up to "outshine," furthermore, a skilled bodhisattva, even though not engaged in material objects, possesses merit through skill in means; by rejoicing in the objects of merit of those in cyclic existence and nirvana, and by dedicating that merit arising from rejoicing as a cause for supreme, excellent enlightenment for the sake of sentient beings, through this dedication, they outshine the virtue of all beings, from the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas downwards. For example, even if there were a great heap of inferior gems, a single precious vaiḍūrya gem would outshine that entire collection of gems. Similarly, the heaps of generosity of all beings, from the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas downwards—including their vast fields, times, and material objects—are outshone by the virtue of a bodhisattva that arises from subsequent rejoicing.

source: པའི་ཞེས་པ་ནས། ཡང་དག་འདའ་བར་འགྱུར་ཞེས་པའི་བར་གྱིས། དེ་ལྟར་གོང་དུ་བསྟན་པ་བཞིན་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་དྲུག་ལ་སྤྱོད་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའི་སྦྱིན་པས་འགྲོ་བ་དམན་པས་ཡི་དྭགས་ཀྱི་སར་འགྲོ་བ་ཡི། སྐྱེ་བའི་རྒྱུན་གཅོད་ལ། མིར་སྐྱེས་ཀྱང་ལོངས་སྤྱོད་པའི་དབུལ་བ་དང་ནི་དེ་བཞིན་ཉོན་མོངས་པའི་སྒྲིབ་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་རྒྱུན་གཅོད་ཅིང་འཁོར་བ་ན་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའི་སྤྱོད་པ་སྤྱད་པའི་ཚེ་ལོངས་སྤྱོད་མཐའ་ཡས་ཐོབ་པར་འགྱུར་ཞིང༌། སྦྱིན་པ་བཏང་བས་འཕོངས་པས་སྡུག་བསྔལ་བར་འགྱུར་བའི་སེམས་ཅན་རྣམས་བསྡུས་ནས་ཡོངས་སུ་སྨིན་པར་བྱེད་དེ། ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་ཀྱིས་དུད་འགྲོའི་རིགས་ཀྱི་འགྲོ་བ་དུ་མའི་ངོ་བོ་དང༌། མི་ཁོམ་པའི་གནས་བརྒྱད་སྤོང་ཞིང༌། དེ་ཡིས་དལ་བ་དང༌། འབྱོར་པའི་ཆོས་བཅུ་རྟག་ཏུ་རྙེད་པར་འགྱུར་ལ། མི་ཁོམ་བརྒྱད་ནི།དམྱལ་བ་ཡི་དྭགས་བྱོལ་སོང་དང༌། །ཀླ་ཀློ་ཚེ་རིང་ལྷ་དང་ནི། །ལོག་ལྟ་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱིས་སྟོང་པ། །ལྐུགས་པ་འདི་དག་མི་ཁོམ་བརྒྱད། །ཅེས་པའོ། །འབྱོར་པ་བཅུ་ལས་རང་འབྱོར་ལྔ་ནི།ཡུལ་དབུས་སྐྱེས་དང་མི་ལུས་ཐོབ། །དབང་པོ་ཚང་ཞིང་གནས་ལ་དད། །ལས་ཀྱི་མཐའ་མ་ལོག་པའོ། །གཞན་འབྱོར་ལྔ་ནི།སངས་རྒྱས་བྱོན་དང་དེས་ཆོས་གསུངས། །བསྟན་པ་ཡུན་དུ་གནས་པ་དང༌། །ཞེས་གསུངས་ཏེ། ཞུགས་དང་འཇུག་པ་གཞན་དོན་དུ་སྙིང་བརྩེ་བའོ། །ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ལུས་དང་མཐུན་པའི་བཟོད་པ་བསྒོམས་པས་གཞན་དོན་ནུས་པའི་གཟུགས་བཟང་པོ་དམ་པ་རྒྱ་ཆེན་པོ་ཐོབ་པར་འགྱུར་ཏེ། གཞན་གྱི་ཡིད་དུ་འོང་བའི་དཔེ་གསེར་གྱི་མདོག་ལྟར་ཡིད་དུ་སྡུག་ཅིང་འགྲོ་བའི་ལྟ་བའི་འོས་སུ་འགྱུར་རོ། །དགེ་བ་ལ་སྤོགས་པའི་བརྩོན་འགྲུས་ཀྱིས་ནི་དཀར་པོའི་ཡོན་ཏན་གཞན་དོན་བྱེད་པ་འགྲིབ་པར་མི་འགྱུར་ཞིང༌། འབྲས་བུའི་ཆོས་ཡེ་ཤེས་མཐའ་ཡས་པ་དང་མཐར་རྒྱལ་བའི་ཡོན་ཏན་རིན་པོ་ཆེ་ཟད་མི་ཤེས་པའི་བང་མཛོད་རྙེད་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །སེམས་བདེ་བར་གནས་པའི་བསམ་གཏན་གྱིས་ནི། འདོད་པའི་ཡོན་ཏན་ལྔ་ལ་ཞེན་ན་སྨད་པ་ཡིན་པས། དེ་དོར་བར་འགྱུར་ཏེ། ལྷའི་མིག་དང༌། སྔོན་གྱི་གནས་རྗེས་སུ་དྲན་པ་དང༌། ཟག་པ་ཟད་པ་ཡི་དང༌། དོན་རིག་པར་དང་མངོན་པར་ཤེས་པ་དང་ཏིང་ངེ་འཛིན་གྲུབ་བོ། །བདག་མེད་རྟོགས་པའི་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱིས་ནི་ཆོས་རྣམས་ཀྱི་རང་བཞིན་སྟོང་པ་ཉིད་དུ་ཡོངས་སུ་ཤེས་ནས། ཁམས་གསུམ་གྱི་སེམས་ཅན་མ་ལུས་པ་འཁོར་བ་ལས་ཡང་དག་པར་འདའ་བར་འགྱུར་རོ། །དེ་ལྟར་རྒྱུ་གསུམ་སྔོན་དུ་སོང་བའི་འབྲས་བུ་ནི། འབྲས་བུ་སྐབས་བརྒྱད་པའི་དོན།
translation: From the phrase "of the" up to the phrase "will truly transcend," it is said: Just as has been taught above, for a bodhisattva practicing the six perfections, the generosity of a bodhisattva cuts off the continuity of birth that leads to the realm of hungry ghosts due to the lower destinies. Even if born as a human, one cuts off the continuity of all poverty of resources and, likewise, all obscurations of the afflictions. When practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva in samsara, one will attain boundless resources. By giving gifts, one gathers and brings to full maturity those sentient beings who are suffering due to deprivation. Through discipline, one abandons the nature of the many destinies of the animal realm and the eight states of non-freedom, and by that, one will always find the ten endowments and freedoms. The eight states of non-freedom are: "Hell, hungry ghosts, animals, / Barbarians, long-lived gods, / Wrong views, empty of a Buddha, / And the mute—these are the eight non-freedoms." Regarding the ten endowments, the five self-endowments are: "Born in a central land, obtained a human body, / Sense faculties complete, faith in the place, / And the finality of karma is not wrong." The five other-endowments are: "A Buddha has appeared, he has taught the Dharma, / The teaching remains for a long time, and..." It is said: [This refers to] having entered and engaged [in the path] with compassion for the sake of others. By meditating on patience that accords with the body of wisdom, one will attain a supreme, vast, and excellent form capable of benefiting others; it will be as pleasing as the color of gold, which is the example of what is pleasing to others, and one will become worthy of being looked upon. Through the diligence that promotes virtue, one’s white qualities of benefiting others will not diminish, and one will find an inexhaustible treasury of the jewel of the qualities of the ultimate victorious one and the boundless wisdom that is the fruit. Through the meditative concentration of a mind abiding in peace, because attachment to the five qualities of desire is something to be disparaged, one will abandon them, and the divine eye, the recollection of former states, the exhaustion of defilements, the knowledge of meanings, and the superknowledges and meditative concentrations will be accomplished. Through the wisdom that realizes selflessness, having thoroughly understood the nature of all phenomena as emptiness, one will truly transcend samsara, along with all sentient beings of the three realms without exception. Thus, the fruit that follows from these three causes is the meaning of the eighth chapter on the fruit.

heading: ཐུན་མོང་གི་འབྲས་བུ་བསྟན་པ།
translation:
The second point, explaining the common result, is as follows: The essence of the Dharmakāya is the complete maturation of all phenomena of purification and nirvāṇa, and because it is the ultimate realization of the non-apprehension of the nature of things, it becomes the basis for the perfection of the benefit of others. As it is said:
"The Svabhāvikakāya, the Sambhogakāya,
And likewise the other, the Nirmāṇakāya,
The Dharmakāya and its activities—
These are correctly expressed as four aspects."
Thus, this passage teaches the Dharmakāya along with its activities in the manner of the four bodies.

heading: ཐུན་མོང་གི་འབྲས་བུ་བསྟན་པ།
translation: It is said: In this way, having perfected the result through listening to, contemplating, and meditating upon this teaching of the non-apprehending perfection of wisdom path, that bodhisattva, through completely pure enlightened activity, upholds the external container-world of the buddhafields and the internal essence of the pure continuum of sentient beings. They also uphold the continuum of the Buddha, the continuum of the scriptural Dharma, and the continuum of the realized Dharma; likewise, they uphold the continuum of the Sangha who practice, as well as all virtuous phenomena. With this, the explanation of the nature of the Dharma as taught by them is concluded.

heading: སྟོན་པས་བསྟན་པའི་དོན་བསྡུ་བ།
translation: It is said: It is like the precious wish-fulfilling jewel that gathers all the infinite virtues of the Buddhas of the three times. It is the authentic path of the great bodhisattvas, who have gathered all the virtues of the speech of the Tathāgatas. Furthermore, since the nature of sentient beings is primordially pure in all sentient beings universally, the Tathāgata himself has truly spoken of this path so that it may be attained by all sentient beings.

source: ཞེས་གསུངས་ཏེ། འཕགས་པ་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་སྡུད་པ་ཚིགས་སུ་བཅད་པའི་ཊཱི་ཀ་ཡིད་བཞིན་གྱི་ནོར་བུ་རིན་པོ་ཆེ་ལྟ་བུ། ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་རྒྱ་མཚོའི་སྡེ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལས། ཐུགས་ཀྱི་མཆོག་ཟབ་མོའི་དོན་ཉམས་སུ་བླང་བའི་རིམ་པའོ།། སྤྱིར་མདོ་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་འདི་ལ་བཤད་ལུགས་བསམ་གྱིས་མི་ཁྱབ་པ་ཡོད་ཀྱང༌། འདི་ནི་ཕལ་ཆེར་དོན་དམ་པ་སྟོན་པ་ལས། ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལྔ་པོ་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པའི་ཞོར་ལ་སྟོན་པའི་ལུགས་ཀྱིས། སྦྱིན་པའི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་དང༌། དེ་བཞིན་དུ་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལྔ་པོའི་སྔོན་དུ། ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་གྲོགས་བྱེད་ཅིང༌། གཞན་པའི་ལུགས་ཀྱིས་སྦྱིན་པ་ནས་རིམ་གྱིས་བརྩམས་ཏེ། གཙོ་བོ་དང༌། ཕལ་བའི་རིམ་པས་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་རྗེས་སུ་འགྲོ་ཡང༌། འདིར་བདག་གི་ཤེས་རབ་མེད་ན་རིམ་གྱིས་འཇུག་མི་ཤེས་པའི་ཕྱིར། དེ་ཅི་སྟེ་ཞེ་ན། ཤེས་རབ་སྔོན་དུ་འགྲོ་བའོ། །དེ་ཅི་སྟེ་ཞེ་ན། མདོ་སྡེ་ཡོན་ཏན་རིན་པོ་ཆེ་བསྡུད་པ་ཚིགས་སུ་བཅད་པའི་སྤྱི་ཡིས་ཀྱང་དེ་ལྟར་བསྟན་ལ། སྒོས་སུ་ཡང་སྦྱིན་པ་བྱིན་པའི་སྔོན་དུ་འགྲོ་བ་ཤེས་རབ་སྟེ། ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་བཟོད་པ། བརྩོན་འགྲུས་བསམ་གཏན་དེ་བཞིན་ནོ། །ཞེས་བཤད་དོ། །འོ་ན་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་འདིའི་རྗེས་ལ་མི་འབྱུང་ངམ་ཞེ་ན་དེ་ནི་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལྔ་པོ་དང་མཉམ་དུ་འབྱུང་ལ། རྟོགས་ཚུལ་གྱི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་ན། རྗེས་སུ་ཡང་འབྱུང་ངོ༌། །དེ་ནི་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་སྤྱིའི་རྣམ་བཞག་གོ །ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་མདོ་རིན་པོ་ཆེ་སྡུད་པ་ཚིགས་སུ་བཅད་པ་རྫོགས་སོ། །
translation: It is said: In the *Ocean of the Perfection of Wisdom*, a commentary on the *Noble Verse Summary of the Perfection of Wisdom* which is like a precious wish-fulfilling jewel, there is the sequence for practicing the profound meaning of the supreme mind. Generally, although there are inconceivable ways of explaining this *Perfection of Wisdom* sutra, this text mostly teaches the ultimate meaning. According to the system that teaches the five perfections as auxiliary to the *perfection of wisdom*, the *perfection of wisdom* acts as a companion prior to the *perfection of generosity* and, likewise, prior to the other five perfections. According to other systems, one begins gradually from generosity, and the *perfection of wisdom* follows in a sequence of primary and secondary importance. However, here, because one cannot know how to enter into the sequence without the wisdom of the self, why is that? It is because wisdom goes first. Why is that? The *Sutra of the Precious Verse Summary of Virtues* teaches it in this general way, and specifically, it teaches that wisdom precedes the giving of generosity, and likewise for ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration. Thus it is explained. If one asks, "Does it not then appear after this *perfection of wisdom*?" the answer is that it does not. It arises simultaneously with the five perfections, and when considered in terms of the mode of realization, it also arises subsequently. This is the general presentation of the *perfection of wisdom*. The *Sutra of the Precious Verse Summary of the Perfection of Wisdom* is concluded.

[2-315] translation already produced for this document:
It is said: From the phrase "he who acts to heal the illnesses of beings" up to the phrase "this is what he has taught," the purpose of those things mentioned above is what is called the "illnesses of beings." Because individuals who do not know this reality of non-apprehension have entered into perverted views, the omniscient teacher, who has become the supreme physician, acts to heal them by establishing them in the reality of emptiness. He has taught this, which is endowed with the profound path of complete enlightenment that teaches the wisdom of non-apprehension, and thus it has been taught correctly. With this, the nature of the six perfections, beginning with the perfection of wisdom, has been explained.

[2-316] translation already produced for this document:
It is said: It is like the precious wish-fulfilling jewel that gathers all the infinite virtues of the Buddhas of the three times. It is the authentic path of the great bodhisattvas, who have gathered all the virtues of the speech of the Tathāgatas. Furthermore, since the nature of sentient beings is primordially pure in all sentient beings universally, the Tathāgata himself has truly spoken of this path so that it may be attained by all sentient beings.

heading: སྟོན་པས་བསྟན་པའི་དོན་བསྡུ་བ།
translation:
Thus, the Blessed One, the Great Lion, from the vast, sky-like treasury of the holy Dharma,
From this teaching, for the sake of taming sentient beings,
The eighty-four thousand holy Dharma, the secret treasury,
For those sentient beings in cyclic existence who do not understand its meaning,
Through the compassion of all the Buddhas of the three times,
From the lineages of the secret, definitive, and interpretive meanings,
The holy Dharma that liberates those of keen faculties,
The supreme and perfect one among the perfections,
This precious essence, which gathers all without exception,
Is the meaning spoken by the Blessed One, the Great Lion,
The supreme intention of the bodhisattvas.
By the virtue of writing this, may all the infinite hosts of sentient beings,
Spanning the reaches of the sky,
Together with this supreme perfection of wisdom,
Realize this supreme and perfect meaning.
This supreme perfection of wisdom,
In the year of the wish-fulfilling tree and the supreme dancer,
On the mountain of the king of birds, the place of prophecy and transformation,
In this great and supreme place of accomplishment,
Through the supreme power of the compassion of the Lord Avalokiteśvara,
I have realized and clearly set down these supreme and perfect words.
May auspicious glory flourish and become an ornament to the world.
May the purpose of this book be fulfilled for the sake of countless sentient beings.
Virtue.

ཞེས་གསུངས་ཏེ། དཔེར་ན་ནོར་བུ་ཞེས་པ་ནས། བྱང་ཆུབ་རེག་ཅེས་པའི་བར་ལ། ནོར་བུའི་དཔེ་དེ་བཞིན་དུ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་འདི་ལ་བརྟེན་ནས་ཡོན་ཏན་ཐམས་ཅད་འབྱུང་བས་མྱུར་དུ་བྱང་ཆུབ་ལ་རེག་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །

[2-104] translation:
It is said: From the passage "like a jewel" up to "touch enlightenment," it should be understood that, just like the analogy of the jewel, a bodhisattva who relies upon this perfection of wisdom, from which all qualities arise, will swiftly touch enlightenment.

[2-101] source:
ཞེས་གསུངས་ཏེ། མི་ཞིག་རྒྱ་མཚོ་ཞེས་པ་ནས། བདག་རེག་འགྱུར་ཞེས་པའི་བར་ལ། རྒྱ་མཚོའི་དཔེ་དེ་ལྟར་བྱང་ཆུབ་དམ་པར་བསྒྲུབ་པའི་ལམ་ལ་རབ་ཏུ་ཞུགས་ཏེ་རྒྱལ་བའི་ཡུམ་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པའི་གླེགས་བམ་འདི་ཉིད་ཡིན་པར་རིག་པར་བྱས་ལ། དེ་ནི་རྣམ་པར་འདྲེན་པས་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཏུ་ལུང་བསྟན་པར་མ་གྱུར་ཀྱང༌། འདི་ནས་བཤད་པ་དང་བདག་གི་བློ་མཐུན་པར་འདུག་པས། དེ་ཡང་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་བྱང་ཆུབ་དེ་དུས་རིང་པོ་མི་ཐོགས་པར་བདག་གིས་རེག་ཅིང་ཐོབ་པར་འགྱུར་རོ་སྙམ་དུ་བལྟའོ། །
[2-101] translation already produced for this document:
It is said: From the passage "like a person in the ocean" up to "I shall touch," it should be understood that, just like the analogy of the ocean, one has entered into the path of accomplishing supreme enlightenment and has recognized that this very volume is the Mother of the Victors, the perfection of wisdom. Even if one has not been prophesied to enlightenment by the Guides, because what is explained here accords with one's own mind, one should view it with the thought: "I shall touch and attain that Buddha-enlightenment without taking a long time."

[2-102] source:
ཅེས་གསུངས་ཏེ། དཔྱིད་དུས་བཟང་ལ་ཞེས་པ་ནས། བྱང་ཆུབ་འཐོབ་ཅེས་པའི་བར་ལ། སྡོང་པོའི་དཔེ་ལྟར་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པའི་གླེགས་བམ་འདི་གང་ཟག་སུའི་ལག་ཏུ་ཐོབ་ཅིང་ཐོས་པ་ལ་སོགས་བྱས་པས་དུས་རིང་པོར་མི་ཐོགས་པར་འདྲེན་པ་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་བྱང་ཆུབ་འཐོབ་བོ། །
[2-102] translation already produced for this document:
It is said: From the passage "in the beautiful spring season" up to "attain enlightenment," it should be understood that, just like the analogy of the tree, whoever obtains this volume of the perfection of wisdom in their hands and engages in listening to it and so forth, will attain the enlightenment of the Guides without taking a long time.

[2-103] source:
ཅེས་གསུངས་ཏེ། དཔེར་ན་བུད་མེད་ཞེས་པ་ནས། བྱང་ཆུབ་རེག་ཅེས་པའི་བར་ལ། སྦྲུམ་མའི་དཔེ་དེ་བཞིན་དུ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་རྒྱལ་བའི་ཡུམ་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་འདི་ཉན་ཅིང་ཐོས་པས་ཆོས་ལ་དགའ་བ་དང་འབྲས་བུ་ལ་འདུན་པ་བསྐྱེད་པས་མྱུར་དུ་བྱང་ཆུབ་ལ་རེག་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །
[2-103] translation already produced for this document:
It is said: From the passage "like a woman" up to "touch enlightenment," it should be understood that, just like the analogy of the pregnant woman, a bodhisattva who listens to and hears this Mother of the Victors, the perfection of wisdom, generates joy for the Dharma and aspiration for the fruit, and thereby will swiftly touch enlightenment.
